# PhotonHTTP documentation (full text)

> PhotonHTTP is a fast, modular HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 web server for macOS 15 and later, written in Swift 6 with Swift Concurrency and no package dependencies. Run it as the `photon` command, configured by one JSON file, or compose its components into your own Swift server.

Every page of https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/ as markdown, in reading order. Links point at the site.


---

<!-- Source: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/getting-started.md (HTML: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/getting-started.html) -->

# Getting started

Install the `photon` command, serve a folder, then grow into a config file when you need TLS,
compression, logs or more than one site.

## Requirements

- macOS 15 or later. PhotonHTTP is built on Darwin and Network.framework and is not built or
  tested on Linux.
- A Swift 6.4 toolchain, from Xcode or [swift.org](https://www.swift.org/install/macos/). The
  installer builds from source.

## Install

One command clones [the repository](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP), builds a
release binary with your Swift toolchain and installs `photon` to `~/.local/bin`. It needs no
sudo.

```bash
curl -fsSL https://photon-http.sstools.co/install.sh | bash
```

Pass options after `bash -s --`:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://photon-http.sstools.co/install.sh | bash -s -- --prefix ~/opt --version main
```

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--prefix DIR` | Install to `DIR/bin` instead of `~/.local/bin`. It must be writable: the installer never uses sudo |
| `--version REF` | The git tag or branch to build. Default `main` |

From a checkout of the repository, run the same installer directly:

```bash
scripts/install.sh
```

Check that your shell finds it:

```bash
photon --help
```

If it says `command not found`, `~/.local/bin` is not on your `PATH` yet. Add it in
`~/.zshrc`:

```bash
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

**Uninstall** by deleting the binary: `rm ~/.local/bin/photon` (or `DIR/bin/photon` with
`--prefix`). It has no other files and no dependencies outside the system.

## Serve a folder

`photon serve` serves a directory as a static website: the current directory unless you name
one. `/` and every directory serve their `index.html`.

```bash
cd ~/Sites/example
photon serve
# listening 127.0.0.1:8080
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8080/` in a browser, or check it with `curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/`.
Press Ctrl-C to stop the server.

```
photon serve [DIR] [--port PORT] [--host HOST]
```

| Argument | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `DIR` | current directory | The directory to serve |
| `--port PORT` | `8080` | The port to listen on; `0` picks any free port (the `listening` line shows which) |
| `--host HOST` | `127.0.0.1` | The address to bind. `127.0.0.1` means only this Mac can connect; `0.0.0.0` shares the site on your network |

```bash
photon serve public --port 8000          # serve ./public on port 8000
photon serve ~/Sites/example --port 0    # any free port
photon serve . --host 0.0.0.0            # reachable from other devices on your network
```

`photon serve` always does plain static serving: it ignores any `http-config.json` in the
folder. With the macOS firewall on, the first time a newly built `photon` listens on `0.0.0.0`
macOS asks whether to accept incoming connections; see
[binding to all interfaces and the firewall prompt](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#binding-to-all-interfaces-and-the-firewall-prompt).

## When you need more: a config file

TLS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, compression, access logs, virtual hosts, authentication and the reverse
proxy are configured in one JSON file, `http-config.json`, which you pass with
`photon --config`. Every key is optional; relative paths resolve against the file's directory.

```json
{
  "root": "public",
  "compression": true,
  "caching": { "maxAge": 600 },
  "errorPages": { "404": "errors/404.html" },
  "accessLog": { "path": "logs/access.log", "format": "combined" }
}
```

```bash
photon --config http-config.json
# listening 127.0.0.1:8080
```

A running server picks up edits to the file by itself, or on SIGHUP, without dropping
requests. `photon check` validates a config, and `photon reload`, `photon status` and
`photon restart` talk to the running server. Every key and command is in
[Running on a Mac](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md).

## Next steps

- [Static websites](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/static-sites.md): caching and ETags, Range, error pages, compression,
  virtual hosts and authentication.
- [Running on a Mac](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md): every command and config key, certificates, ports
  80 and 443, LaunchAgents, logs, reload.
- [TLS](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/tls.md): HTTPS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 with a PKCS#12 identity loaded in memory, never the
  keychain.
- [Dynamic websites](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/dynamic-sites.md): proxy paths to a local app, or write handlers in Swift
  with Router and WebSockets.
- [Choosing components](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md): build your own server as a Swift package from
  the parts you need.
- [Overview and architecture](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/overview.md): how the pieces fit.

<!-- Source: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/overview.md (HTML: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/overview.html) -->

# Overview and architecture

PhotonHTTP is an HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 server for **macOS 15 or later**, written in
Swift 6 with strict concurrency and **no package dependencies**. It uses Darwin (POSIX sockets,
kqueue, `sendfile(2)`, zlib, libcompression) and Network.framework (TLS, QUIC). It is not built
or tested on Linux.

It comes in two forms:

- **The `photon` executable**: one binary configured by a JSON file
  (`http-config.json`). It serves static files and reverse-proxies paths to local apps, over
  cleartext HTTP/1.1, HTTPS (HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2) and HTTP/3 at once. See
  [Running on a Mac](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md).
- **A set of library products** you compose in your own Swift package, adding in-process
  handlers (a `Router`, WebSockets) to whichever components you want. See
  [Choosing components](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md).

## Core and optional components

The design rule (ROADMAP §1.1) is a minimal core plus optional components, each in its own
target. A component that is not registered is not in the compiled request path at all.

| Layer | Targets | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Core | `HTTPCore` | Bytes (`ByteBuffer`), header fields, `HTTPRequest`/`HTTPResponse`, the `HTTPHandler` and `HTTPMiddleware` protocols, the middleware builder, transport protocols, `RequestContext` |
| Core | `HTTP1` | HTTP/1.1 parser, serializer, chunked codec, connection state machine and runner |
| Core | `HTTPServer` | `Server`: listeners, protocol registry, connection limit, lifecycle and graceful drain |
| Core | `NetworkTransport` | Listeners and connections: BSD sockets + kqueue, Network.framework TCP, TLS and QUIC |
| Protocols | `HPACK` + `HTTP2`, `QPACK` + `HTTP3` (both on `HeaderCompression`), `WebSockets` | Optional protocols |
| Components | `StaticFiles` (includes `ErrorPages`), `Compression`, `VirtualHosts`, `Auth`, `AccessLog`, `Router`, `Proxy` | Optional request-path features |
| Glue | `ConfigFile` | `http-config.json` → settings → listeners, protocols and middleware chain (uses Foundation, startup only) |
| Tools | `photon`, `sws-bench`, `HTTPTestSupport` | The shipped server, the benchmark harness, in-memory test transports |

The [component table](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md#targets-and-products) lists dependencies and when
to include each one.

## Protocols

| Protocol | Listener | How a connection gets it |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP/1.1 | cleartext TCP and TLS | Always available. Keep-alive, pipelining, chunked and `Content-Length` bodies, `Expect: 100-continue` |
| HTTP/2 | TLS (ALPN `h2`) | The TLS listener offers `h2` and `http/1.1` through ALPN; the client picks. Optional cleartext h2c with prior knowledge (`"http2": {"cleartext": true}`), which makes every cleartext connection sniff its first bytes. h2c `Upgrade` and server push are not supported (removed from RFC 9113 / dropped by browsers) |
| HTTP/3 | QUIC (UDP) | A separate QUIC listener, by default on the TLS port number over UDP. HTTPS responses carry `Alt-Svc: h3=":PORT"; ma=SECONDS` so browsers discover it; cleartext and HTTP/3 responses do not |
| WebSockets | any | RFC 6455 Upgrade on HTTP/1.1, extended CONNECT on HTTP/2 (RFC 8441) and HTTP/3 (RFC 9220) |

Protocol choice happens once per connection, by ALPN on TLS and QUIC or by the first bytes on
cleartext. The handler chain is the same for every protocol, so a component written once
serves h1, h2 and h3.

HTTP/2 passes the h2spec conformance suite (146/146) and has limits against the known HTTP/2
attacks (rapid reset, CONTINUATION, control-frame floods, slow reads). HTTP/3 has QPACK (static
table by default, dynamic table opt-in), control streams, RFC 9218 priorities and a `GOAWAY`
drain. One known Network.framework limitation: an HTTP/3 application close code never reaches
the wire (see [notes/nw-transport.md](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/notes/nw-transport.md)). There is no 0-RTT.

## Transports

| Transport | Used for | Type |
|---|---|---|
| BSD sockets + kqueue | cleartext TCP (default, `"transport": "bsd"`) | `BSDSocketListener` |
| Network.framework `NWListener` | cleartext TCP when `"transport": "nw"` | `TCPListener` |
| Network.framework TLS | HTTPS (TLS 1.2+, ALPN) | `TCPListener(configuration:tls:)` |
| Network.framework QUIC | HTTP/3 | `QUICListener` |

Cleartext defaults to BSD sockets because Network.framework connection setup costs about
665 µs and 409 allocations per connection, serialized on one queue; the BSD listener accepts
about 22k new connections per second, on par with nginx (decision #0113,
[M3-accept](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/M3-accept.md)). TLS and QUIC stay on Network.framework, which
supplies TLS 1.3, QUIC, loss recovery and congestion control. Large static files go out with
`sendfile(2)` on the BSD transport.

TLS identities are PKCS#12 files loaded **in memory only** (`SecPKCS12Import` with
`kSecImportToMemoryOnly`); the server never reads or writes a keychain.

## Concurrency model

- One task per connection, no actors on the request path. Lifetimes are a task-group tree:
  server → listener → connection → stream. There are no unstructured `Task {}`s.
- Every protocol layer is a value-type state machine (`mutating func handle(_ event:) ->
  Action`, no I/O), tested over in-memory transports.
- Reads are demand-driven: nothing reads ahead of the handler, so a slow consumer applies TCP
  (or QUIC stream) backpressure. No unbounded buffers.
- The hot path parses bytes directly, with no `String` or Foundation work and no allocations in
  the server's own code (`sws-bench` counts them).
- Shared HTTP/2 connection state is a `Mutex` with non-suspending critical sections.

## Requests, handlers and the chain

```swift
public protocol HTTPHandler: Sendable {
    func handle(_ request: HTTPRequest, context: RequestContext) async throws -> HTTPResponse
}
public protocol HTTPMiddleware: Sendable {
    func handle<Next: HTTPHandler>(_ request: HTTPRequest, context: RequestContext,
                                   next: Next) async throws -> HTTPResponse
}
```

A response body is `.empty`, `.bytes(ByteBuffer)`, `.stream(length:writer:)` (written under
backpressure), `.file(FileRegion)` (sent with `sendfile`) or `.tunnel` (take over the byte
stream: WebSockets and proxied upgrades). An `HTTPRequest` is valid only while `handle` runs;
`snapshot()` copies it.

`Server` takes a `@MiddlewareBuilder` block. The builder turns the list into one nested
generic type at compile time, so the chain is statically dispatched and an `if` that leaves a
component out costs one predictable branch. Order is onion order: the first element sees the
request first and the response last; the last element is the handler. Details:
[MIDDLEWARE.md](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/MIDDLEWARE.md).

### The chain the executable builds

`ServerSettings.makeHandler()` (target `ConfigFile`) registers only the enabled components, in
this order:

| # | Component | Config key | Why here |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `AltSvc` | `http3` | Adds `Alt-Svc` to HTTPS responses |
| 2 | `AccessLog` | `accessLog` | Outermost, so it records final statuses: error pages, auth rejections, proxied responses |
| 3 | `MetricsEndpoint` | `accessLog.metrics` | Answers `GET /metrics` before anything else runs |
| 4 | `Compression` | `compression` | Outside error pages, so generated pages are compressed too |
| 5 | `ErrorPages` | `errorPages` | Fills bodiless `4xx`/`5xx` from everything inside it (auth `401`, proxy `502`/`504`, files `404`) |
| 6 | `Authenticator` | `auth` | Before the proxy, so protected paths are checked before anything is forwarded |
| 7 | `ReverseProxy` | `proxy` | Matches mounts; everything else falls through |
| 8 | `StaticFiles` or `VirtualHosts` | `root` / `hosts` | The terminal handler. With `hosts`, each site has its own `StaticFiles` and its own `hosts[].proxy` mounts |

A request for `/api/items` with `proxy` and `auth` configured walks: access log → compression →
error pages → auth check → proxy (match: forwarded upstream). A request for `/style.css` walks
the same way and falls through the proxy to the static files.

## Lifecycle

`Server.run()` binds every listener in order (cleartext, then TLS, then QUIC), runs until
`requestShutdown()` and returns after a graceful drain: listeners stop accepting, every
connection's shutdown signal fires (HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send `GOAWAY`, WebSockets close with
1001), and open connections get up to `drainTimeout` to finish before they are cancelled. The
executable maps SIGINT and SIGTERM to that drain. See
[Running on a Mac](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#shutdown-restart-and-reload).


---

<!-- Source: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md (HTML: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.html) -->

# Running on a Mac

## Install

```bash
curl -fsSL https://photon-http.sstools.co/install.sh | bash
```

The installer clones the repository, builds a release `photon` with your Swift toolchain and
installs it to `~/.local/bin/photon`. It never uses `sudo`; if `~/.local/bin` is not on your
`PATH` it prints the line to add. Options (after `bash -s --`):

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--prefix DIR` | Install to `DIR/bin` instead of `~/.local/bin` (must be writable) |
| `--version REF` | Git tag or branch to build (default `main`) |

From a checkout, `scripts/install.sh` builds and installs that checkout. Run the installer
again to update. Uninstall with `rm ~/.local/bin/photon`.

Requirements: macOS 15 or later and a Swift 6.4 toolchain (Xcode or swift.org).

### Build by hand

```bash
swift build -c release -j 2 --product photon     # or scripts/build.sh
.build/release/photon --help
```

The binary has no dependencies outside the system, so you can copy `.build/release/photon`
anywhere, e.g. `/usr/local/bin` or `~/bin`.

## Serve a folder

```bash
cd ~/Sites/my-site
photon serve                        # http://127.0.0.1:8080/
photon serve ~/Sites/blog --port 9000
```

```
photon serve [DIR] [--port PORT] [--host HOST]
```

`photon serve` serves `DIR` (default: the current directory) as a static website. A request
for `/` or any directory serves its `index.html`; a directory requested without the trailing
slash redirects to it. `--port` defaults to `8080` (`0` picks a free one) and `--host` to
`127.0.0.1`, so only this Mac can connect; `--host 0.0.0.0` shares the site with your network
(see [the firewall prompt](#binding-to-all-interfaces-and-the-firewall-prompt)). It prints
`listening HOST:PORT` once ready; Ctrl-C stops.

`serve` never reads `http-config.json`, so a stray config file cannot change what it does.
For HTTPS, compression, access logs, error pages or virtual hosts, write a config and run
`photon --config FILE` (below).

## Command line

```
photon [--config FILE] [--root DIR] [--host HOST] [--port PORT]
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--config FILE` | The JSON config. Without it: `$ROOT_PATH/http-config.json` when `ROOT_PATH` is set, else `./http-config.json` if it exists, else built-in defaults |
| `--root DIR` | Directory to serve; overrides `root`. Relative to the working directory |
| `--host HOST` | Numeric address to bind; overrides `host` |
| `--port PORT` | Cleartext port; overrides `port`. `0` picks a free one |
| `--help`, `-h` | Usage |

`--flag=value` works too. Output:

- stderr: `photon: serving /abs/root` (or one line per virtual host), config warnings,
  `signal 15, shutting down`, `stopped`, and errors.
- stdout: `listening 127.0.0.1:8080` once bound, then `listening 127.0.0.1:8443 (https)` and
  `listening 127.0.0.1:8443 (h3)` for the other listeners. Scripts can wait for the first line.
  The access log also goes to stdout when configured that way.

Exit status: `0` after a graceful stop, `1` on a configuration or startup error (bad value,
missing root, unreadable identity, port in use) with a message naming the key, `2` on a usage
error.

### Control commands

The same executable checks a config and talks to a running server (#0143). It finds the server
through its status file (`statusFile`, default `run/status.json` next to the config) and
signals its pid; there is no control socket, so nothing new is reachable over the network.

```
photon check   [--config FILE] [--root DIR] [--host HOST] [--port PORT]
photon reload  [--config FILE] [--root DIR] [--host HOST] [--port PORT] [--timeout SECONDS]
photon status  [--config FILE] [--json]
photon restart [--config FILE] [--root DIR] [--host HOST] [--port PORT] [--timeout SECONDS]
```

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `check` | Loads and builds the config as a reload would (root, error pages, credential files, the TLS identity in memory only) and prints `PATH: valid` or `PATH: invalid: …`. When a server runs with this config, it also prints which keys would change: `can hot-reload: root changed`, `no setting changes` (a reload still rereads the identity and credential files), or `needs a restart: port changed and needs a restart; run `photon restart` to apply them` |
| `reload` | Runs `check`; when the config is valid and needs no restart, sends SIGHUP and waits (up to `--timeout`, default 10 s) for the server to record the outcome, then prints `reloaded: …`, `reload failed, …` or `reload rejected, …`. It does not signal when the config is invalid or needs a restart |
| `status` | Prints the status file: state and pid, listening addresses, config path and SHA-256, the last reload (time, `signal` or `watch`, result, message), the reload count and any restart-required keys. `--json` prints the file itself |
| `restart` | Runs `check`; when the config is valid (whether or not it needs a restart), sends SIGUSR2 and waits (up to `--timeout`, default 10 s) for the outcome: `restarted (changed: port); listening …` or `restart failed, the running server keeps serving: …`. The [graceful restart](#graceful-restart) happens in the same process, so launchd sees one pid. It does not signal when the config is invalid |

Without `--root`/`--host`/`--port`, `check`, `reload` and `restart` apply the overrides the
running server was started with (recorded in the status file). Exit status: `0` success, `1`
invalid config, no running server, a failed reload or restart, or a timeout, `2` usage error,
`3` a restart is required (the reload was or would be rejected).

The status file is JSON, rewritten atomically (temporary file, then rename) with mode 0600 at
startup once the listeners are bound, after every reload and restart and at a clean exit
(`"state": "stopped"`). It holds `pid`, `started`, `config`, `configSHA256` (of the file as
last loaded), `arguments`, `listening`, `reloads` (reloads and restarts), `lastReload`
(`time`, `trigger`: `signal` / `watch` / `restart`, `result`: `reloaded` / `failed` /
`rejected` / `restarted`, `message`, `changed`, `restartRequired`), `restarted` (time of the
last graceful restart), `restartRequired` (keys changed in the file but not applied; empty
after a successful reload or restart) and `settings`: a digest per key of the running values, never the values themselves,
so `check` can compare without the file holding passwords. It is written only when the server
runs with a config file.

## `http-config.json` reference

The file is one JSON object. **Every key is optional**: a missing key keeps its default, so
`{}` (or no file) is a valid config serving `./Public` on `127.0.0.1:8080`. Unknown keys print
a warning and are ignored. A wrong type or out-of-range value stops the server (exit 1) with a
message such as `"timeouts.idle" must be a number of seconds`. **Relative paths resolve
against the directory holding the config file** (except `--root`).

Durations are numbers of seconds (fractions allowed, at most one year). For the HTTP/1.1
`timeouts` and the proxy's `proxy[].timeouts` (`connect`, `response`, `idle`, `total`), `0` or
`null` turns a limit off; leaving a key out keeps its default. Turn off the proxy's `idle` and
`response` limits (or set them large) for long-polling or streaming upstreams such as
server-sent events.

[`Root/http-config.json`](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Root/http-config.json) spells out the core defaults;
[`Root/http-config.tls.json`](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Root/http-config.tls.json) adds HTTPS and HTTP/3;
[`Root/http-config.proxy.json`](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Root/http-config.proxy.json) adds a reverse-proxy mount.

### Listening and limits

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `host` | string | `"127.0.0.1"` | Numeric address to bind. `"0.0.0.0"` (IPv4) or `"::"` serves the network |
| `port` | integer 0–65535 | `8080` | Cleartext TCP port; `0` picks one |
| `transport` | `"bsd"` \| `"nw"` | `"bsd"` | Cleartext transport: POSIX sockets + kqueue, or Network.framework |
| `maxConnections` | integer ≥ 1 | `1024` | Connections served at once across all listeners; more wait in the listen backlog |
| `maxBodySize` | integer bytes | `10485760` | Largest request body (`413` above). Legacy alias `maxRequestSize` |
| `timeouts` | object | see below | HTTP/1.1 time limits in seconds |
| `timeouts.header` | seconds | `10` | Request head must complete (`408`) |
| `timeouts.idle` | seconds | `5` | Idle keep-alive connection closed; also an idle HTTP/2 connection (`GOAWAY`). Legacy `keepAliveTimeout` |
| `timeouts.body` | seconds | `30` | Longest wait for request body bytes (`408`) |
| `timeouts.send` | seconds | `30` | Longest wait for the client to accept response bytes |
| `timeouts.linger` | seconds | `2` | Lingering close after an error response |
| `drainTimeout` | seconds or `null` | `10` | Graceful stop waits this long for open connections; `null` waits indefinitely (`0` cancels at once) |
| `reload` | bool or object | `{"watch": true, "interval": 2}` | Hot reload when the config or a file it names changes ([reload](#shutdown-restart-and-reload)). `false` reloads on SIGHUP only |
| `reload.watch` | bool | `true` | Poll the files with `stat` and reload on a change |
| `reload.interval` | seconds 0.01–3600 | `2` | Time between polls |
| `statusFile` | path, `false` or `null` | `"run/status.json"` | Status file for the [control commands](#control-commands), relative to the config's directory; `false` turns it off |

### Files

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `root` | string | `"Public"` | Directory to serve. Legacy alias `path` |
| `index` | string or array | `["index.html"]` | Index files tried in order for a directory. Legacy alias `defaultIndex` |
| `mimeTypes` | object | `{}` | Extra or overriding types: `{"md": "text/markdown; charset=utf-8"}`. The legacy array form `[{"contentType": …, "pathExtensions": […]}]` is accepted |
| `defaultMimeType` | string | `"application/octet-stream"` | For unknown extensions |
| `blockList` | array of strings | `["http-config.json", ".git", ".DS_Store"]` | Path components answered `403` anywhere in the path, case-insensitively |
| `blockDotfiles` | bool | `true` | `403` for any component starting with `.`, except `.well-known` |
| `caching` | bool or object | `{"enabled": true, "maxAge": 3600}` | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=N` on files and `304`s; `false` or `"enabled": false` sends none |
| `errorPages` | bool or object | `true` | `true`: generated HTML pages for bodiless `4xx`/`5xx`; `false`: none; `{"404": "errors/404.html"}`: files relative to `root` (other statuses keep the generated page); with `hosts`, each site's root first, then `root` |
| `compression` | bool or object | off | See [Compression](#compression) |
| `enableETags` | – | – | Legacy, no effect (ETags are always sent); accepted with a warning |
| `enableCompression` | bool | – | Legacy; `true` is `"compression": true` (ignored when `compression` is set) |

### Compression

`"compression": true` uses every default, or an object:

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | bool | `true` | `false` turns it off |
| `encodings` | array | `["br", "gzip", "deflate"]` | Codings offered, from `br`, `gzip`, `deflate` |
| `minimumSize` | integer bytes | `1024` | Smaller bodies are sent as they are |
| `level` | integer 1–9 | `4` | zlib level for per-response gzip/deflate |
| `precompressionLevel` | integer 1–9 | `9` | Level for static-file variants compressed once into the cache |
| `mimeTypes` | array | `text/*`, JSON, JavaScript, XML (incl. SVG), wasm, YAML, TOML, some fonts and icons | Types that are compressed; `*` wildcards allowed |
| `precompress` | bool | `true` | Compress small static files once into the file cache |
| `sidecars` | bool | `true` | Serve `file.br` / `file.gz` next to a file as its variants |

### TLS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tls` | object, `false` or `null` | off | HTTPS listener |
| `tls.identity` | string (required) | – | PKCS#12 file (certificate chain + key), relative to the config file. Loaded in memory only |
| `tls.password` | string | – | Its password; or |
| `tls.passwordEnv` | string | – | Name of an environment variable holding the password (exactly one of the two) |
| `tls.port` | integer | `8443` | TCP port; must differ from `port`; `0` picks one |
| `tls.enabled` | bool | `true` | `false` turns it off |
| `http2` | bool or object | on | HTTP/2. On by default (offered on HTTPS via ALPN); `false` or `"enabled": false` serves HTTP/1.1 only |
| `http2.cleartext` | bool | `false` | Also accept h2c with prior knowledge on the cleartext port (every cleartext connection is then sniffed) |
| `http2.maxConcurrentStreams` | integer 0–65536 | `100` | `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS` |
| `http2.initialWindowSize` | integer 0–2147483647 | `65535` | Per-stream receive window |
| `http2.maxRequestBodySize` | integer or `null` | `maxBodySize` | Largest request body on HTTP/2 |
| `http2.abuseLimits` | object | defaults | DoS limits (counts per `window`; `null` turns one off): `window` (s, 10), `maxResetStreamsPerWindow` (100), `maxControlFramesPerWindow` (1000), `maxEmptyFramesPerWindow` (100), `maxWindowUpdatesPerWindow` (10000), `maxSmallDataFramesPerWindow` (1000), `smallDataFrameSize` (256), `windowStallTimeout` (s, 30), `maxStreamsPerConnection` (100000). Background: [HTTP2.md](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/HTTP2.md) |
| `http3` | bool or object | off | HTTP/3 over QUIC; **needs `tls`**. `true` = defaults |
| `http3.port` | integer or `null` | TLS port number | UDP port (the same number as HTTPS is normal: TCP and UDP do not clash) |
| `http3.altSvcMaxAge` | integer seconds | `86400` | `ma` of the `Alt-Svc` header on HTTPS responses |
| `http3.qpackMaxTableCapacity` | integer 0–1048576 | `0` | QPACK dynamic table offered to clients; `0` = static table only |
| `http3.qpackBlockedStreams` | integer 0–1000 | `0` | Streams that may wait on QPACK inserts |
| `http3.enabled` | bool | `true` | `false` turns it off |

### Virtual hosts, auth, proxy and logs

These have their own sections:

| Key | Default | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| `hosts` | `[]` | [Virtual hosts](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/static-sites.md#virtual-hosts) |
| `auth` | `[]` | [Authentication](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/static-sites.md#authentication) |
| `proxy` | `[]` | [Reverse proxy reference](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/dynamic-sites.md#proxy-mount-reference) |
| `accessLog` | off | [Logs](#logs) below |

## HTTPS with a PKCS#12 identity

The server loads a PKCS#12 (`.p12`) file holding the certificate chain and private key, in
memory only (`SecPKCS12Import` with `kSecImportToMemoryOnly`). It never touches the keychain,
so nothing prompts and nothing is installed.

```json
{
  "host": "0.0.0.0",
  "port": 80,
  "root": "/Users/me/Sites/example",
  "tls": { "identity": "certs/example.p12", "passwordEnv": "SWS_P12_PASSWORD", "port": 443 },
  "http3": true
}
```

### Local testing

```bash
scripts/make-test-identity.sh            # .test-identity/server.p12, self-signed for localhost
.build/release/photon --config Root/http-config.tls.json
curl -k https://127.0.0.1:8443/                      # HTTP/2 via ALPN
curl -k --http1.1 https://127.0.0.1:8443/
/opt/homebrew/opt/curl/bin/curl --http3-only -k https://127.0.0.1:8443/   # Homebrew curl has HTTP/3
```

Browsers reject a self-signed certificate unless you trust it, which changes the keychain's
trust settings; do that by hand only if you want to, or test with curl.

### A real certificate (Let's Encrypt)

Any ACME client that writes PEM files works, for example [lego](https://go-acme.github.io/lego/),
[acme.sh](https://github.com/acmesh-official/acme.sh) or certbot (all installable with
Homebrew). The HTTP-01 challenge needs the domain to reach this Mac on port 80, and
StaticFiles serves `/.well-known/` even with `blockDotfiles` on, so you can use webroot mode
with your site's `root`:

```bash
# Example with lego, webroot mode, while PhotonHTTP serves the site on port 80
lego --email you@example.com --domains example.com --domains www.example.com \
     --http --http.webroot /Users/me/Sites/example run
# certificates land in ./.lego/certificates/example.com.crt (full chain) and .key
```

Convert to PKCS#12. Use the legacy-compatible algorithms: `SecPKCS12Import` does not reliably
accept OpenSSL 3's default AES/PBKDF2 encryption (this is what `scripts/make-test-identity.sh`
does too):

```bash
export SWS_P12_PASSWORD='a long random password'
openssl pkcs12 -export \
  -inkey example.com.key -in example.com.crt \
  -out certs/example.p12 -passout env:SWS_P12_PASSWORD \
  -keypbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -certpbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -macalg sha1
chmod 600 certs/example.p12
```

`-in` must be the full chain (leaf first, then intermediates). Use Homebrew's
`/opt/homebrew/bin/openssl` if `/usr/bin/openssl` (LibreSSL) rejects an option.

After a renewal, write the new `.p12` over the old path (make it in a temporary file, then
`mv` it into place, so the server never reads half a file) and send **SIGHUP**: the server
rereads the identity, and new HTTPS and HTTP/3 connections get the new certificate without a
restart or dropped connections (see [reload](#shutdown-restart-and-reload)). With the file
watcher on (the default, `reload.watch`), the signal is optional: the server sees the new file
within `reload.interval` and reloads by itself. ACME clients have a renew hook for that, e.g. `kill -HUP "$(pgrep -f 'photon --config /path/to/http-config.json')"`.
stderr confirms it with `reload: TLS identity PATH reloaded`; if the new file does not load
(wrong password, not PKCS#12) it prints `warning: reload: cannot load TLS identity …; keeping
the current TLS certificate` and keeps serving the old one.

## Binding to all interfaces and the firewall prompt

The default `host` is `127.0.0.1`: only this Mac can connect. To serve your network or the
internet, set `"host": "0.0.0.0"` (all IPv4 interfaces) or `"::"`.

With the macOS application firewall on (System Settings → Network → Firewall), the first time
an **unsigned or newly built** binary listens on a non-loopback address macOS asks "Do you want
the application "photon" to accept incoming network connections?". Each rebuild changes
the binary, so the prompt can come back. Options:

- Click Allow once per build (fine on a desktop; it blocks an unattended start under launchd
  until someone clicks).
- Install one stable copy (e.g. `/usr/local/bin/photon`), and allow it once; sign it
  with your own Developer ID (`codesign -s "Developer ID Application: …"`) so the approval
  survives updates.
- Allow it ahead of time from an admin shell:
  `sudo /usr/libexec/ApplicationFirewall/socketfilterfw --add /usr/local/bin/photon`
  and `--unblockapp` the same path.

Loopback (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`) never prompts, which is why every example and test here binds
loopback. A server reached only through a local reverse proxy or a tunnel (Tailscale, Cloudflare
Tunnel) can stay on loopback or bind only the tunnel's address.

HTTP/3 needs the UDP port open as well as TCP, in any firewall or router in front of the Mac.

## Ports 80 and 443 without root

Since macOS 10.14 (Mojave), a non-root process may bind ports below 1024 on the **wildcard**
address, so `"host": "0.0.0.0"` (or `"::"`) with `"port": 80` and `"tls": {"port": 443}` works
as a normal user. Binding a *specific* address below 1024 can still fail with `EACCES`
("Permission denied"); bind the wildcard instead. Do not run the server as root.

## Running as a LaunchAgent

A user LaunchAgent starts the server at login and restarts it if it exits. Save as
`~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.example.photonhttp.plist` (adjust paths):

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key>
  <string>com.example.photonhttp</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>/usr/local/bin/photon</string>
    <string>--config</string>
    <string>/Users/me/Sites/example/http-config.json</string>
  </array>
  <key>WorkingDirectory</key>
  <string>/Users/me/Sites/example</string>
  <key>EnvironmentVariables</key>
  <dict>
    <key>SWS_P12_PASSWORD</key>
    <string>…</string>
  </dict>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key>
  <true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key>
  <dict>
    <key>SuccessfulExit</key>
    <false/>
  </dict>
  <key>ExitTimeOut</key>
  <integer>30</integer>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key>
  <string>/Users/me/Library/Logs/PhotonHTTP/stdout.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key>
  <string>/Users/me/Library/Logs/PhotonHTTP/stderr.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>
```

```bash
mkdir -p ~/Library/Logs/PhotonHTTP
launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.example.photonhttp.plist
photon restart --config /Users/me/Sites/example/http-config.json   # apply a config, no gap
launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.example.photonhttp    # new process (a new binary)
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.example.photonhttp         # stop and unload
```

- **A config change** that a reload rejects (ports, `tls`, `http2`, `http3`, limits) is applied
  with `photon restart`: the [graceful restart](#graceful-restart) runs inside the
  process launchd started, so the job keeps its pid, nothing is refused, and launchd sees no
  exit.
- **A new binary** needs a new process: `launchctl kickstart -k` sends SIGTERM (the server
  drains for up to `drainTimeout`), then launchd starts the new binary. Connections are refused
  from the moment the old listeners close until the new process has bound them, usually well
  under a second. Moving listening sockets into a new process (an `exec`-based hand-off) does
  not fit launchd's model of one job, one pid it started and watches, so it is not done.

- `KeepAlive` with `SuccessfulExit = false` restarts the server after a crash or a startup
  error, but not after a clean stop (exit 0).
- launchd stops a job with SIGTERM and kills it after `ExitTimeOut` seconds (default 20).
  Keep `drainTimeout` (default 10) below it so the drain finishes.
- A LaunchAgent runs only while you are logged in. For a server that runs without a login, a
  LaunchDaemon in `/Library/LaunchDaemons` (needs admin) with `UserName` set to an unprivileged
  account does the same job.
- Keep the site and config **outside** `~/Desktop`, `~/Documents` and `~/Downloads`: those are
  privacy-protected, and a launchd job reading them is denied or triggers a permission prompt.
- The `EnvironmentVariables` password is readable by anyone who can read the plist; keep it
  `chmod 600`, or point `passwordEnv` at a variable you set another way.

## Logs

- **Startup and errors** go to stderr; **`listening` lines** to stdout.
- **Access log**: the `accessLog` key.

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `accessLog` | bool, string or object | off | `true`: Common lines to stdout. A string: the `path`. `false`/`null`: off |
| `accessLog.path` | string or `null` | `"stdout"` | A file (relative to the config file; appended to, created `0644`; its directory must exist), `"stdout"` or `"stderr"`. `null` writes no lines (metrics only) |
| `accessLog.format` | `"common"` \| `"combined"` \| `"json"` | `"common"` | Combined adds `Referer` and `User-Agent`; JSON lines include the duration |
| `accessLog.metrics` | bool or path | off | Serve Prometheus metrics at this path (`true` = `/metrics`) |
| `accessLog.flushInterval` | seconds > 0 | `1` | Longest a line waits in its buffer |
| `accessLog.enabled` | bool | `true` | `false` turns it off |

The access log is outermost in the chain, so it records the final status of every response
(error pages, auth rejections, proxied responses). Lines are buffered per connection and
written by a background task; if the writer falls behind, lines are dropped (counted), never
delayed. A graceful stop writes everything buffered. `metrics` is served to anyone who can
reach the server; protect it with `auth` if that matters.

**Rotation.** The server does not rotate files itself. Move the file aside, then send SIGHUP:
the log is reopened by its path, so the next lines go to a new file and the moved one is
complete once the connections open before the signal have closed (each finishes its buffered
lines into it).

```bash
mv logs/access.log logs/access.log.1
kill -HUP "$(pgrep -f 'photon --config /path/to/http-config.json')"
```

`newsyslog` signals a process through a pid file, which the server does not write; run the two
commands above from a LaunchAgent with `StartCalendarInterval` instead (or have your own
wrapper write a pid file).

## Shutdown, restart and reload

- **SIGUSR2** starts a [graceful restart](#graceful-restart) (what `photon restart`
  sends).
- **SIGINT and SIGTERM** start a graceful shutdown: listeners stop accepting, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
  connections get `GOAWAY`, proxied WebSocket tunnels are closed at the TCP level (clients see
  1006; in-process `WebSocketUpgrade` sessions in a custom server get Close 1001, see
  [WebSockets](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/websockets.md)), in-flight requests finish for up
  to `drainTimeout` seconds, then the rest are cancelled; the access log flushes and the
  process exits 0. A second signal during the drain is harmless. `scripts/sigterm.sh` sends
  SIGTERM to whatever listens on `PORT` (default 8080).
- **Hot reload, no signal needed** (#0142). The server polls `http-config.json` and the files
  it names that a reload reads (the TLS identity, `auth` Basic credential files, `errorPages`
  files) with `stat` every `reload.interval` seconds (default 2). A change of modification
  time, size or inode (an editor or `tailscale cert`/lego renaming a new file into place)
  starts a reload once the files have stopped changing for `min(interval, 0.5 s)`, so a file
  still being written is not read; a file that is malformed when read never replaces the
  running configuration. stderr says `PATH changed, reloading the configuration`. Reloads,
  whether from the watcher or SIGHUP, run one at a time, and none start once the server is
  draining. `"reload": false` turns the watcher off.
- **SIGHUP reloads** `http-config.json` (the same file and command-line overrides as at
  startup) and reopens the access log file. The new configuration is parsed, validated and
  built first; on success new requests use it, while requests already running finish on the
  old one (the old chain, its proxy pools and its log writer are retired once the connections
  opened before the reload have closed). On failure (bad JSON, an unknown key's error, a root
  or error page that cannot be opened, an auth file that cannot be read) stderr says
  `reload failed, keeping the running configuration: …` and nothing changes except the log
  reopen. Success prints `reloaded the configuration`.

  | Reloaded (SIGHUP or the watcher) | Needs a restart (a reload that changes one is rejected whole) |
  |---|---|
  | `root`, `index`, `mimeTypes`, `defaultMimeType`, `blockList`, `blockDotfiles`, `caching`, `errorPages`, `compression`, `hosts`, `auth` (and its credential files), `proxy` and `hosts[].proxy`, `accessLog` (path, format, metrics, flush interval), `reload`, `statusFile`, `tls.identity` and `tls.password` / `tls.passwordEnv` (the identity file is reread on every SIGHUP, so a renewal at the same path is picked up) | `host`, `port`, `transport`, adding or removing `tls`, `tls.port`, `http2`, `http3`, `maxConnections`, `drainTimeout`, `timeouts`, `maxBodySize` |

  The identity reload prints one line: `reload: TLS identity PATH reloaded; new HTTPS and HTTP/3
  handshakes use the new certificate`, `reload: TLS identity PATH unchanged`, or `warning:
  reload: cannot load TLS identity PATH: …; keeping the current TLS certificate`. Open
  connections keep the certificate they negotiated.

  **A restart-only change rejects the whole reload** (#0143): none of the file applies, not
  even its reloadable keys, so the running state always matches one whole config file. stderr
  says `reload rejected, keeping the running configuration: port changed and needs a restart;
  run `photon restart` to apply them`, and the status file records the keys in
  `restartRequired` until a reload succeeds. Every later reload is rejected the same way until
  the file is put back or the server restarts. `photon check` tells you before you
  save or signal. Access log metrics start from zero after a reload (the new chain has its own
  counters). To apply restart-only keys, run `photon restart` (below).
- Static file *contents* need no restart: cached entries are re-checked with `stat` at most
  once per second.

### Graceful restart

`photon restart` (or SIGUSR2 to the server's pid) applies a whole config file,
restart-only keys included, inside the running process (#0144):

1. The server reads, validates and builds the config as at startup (same file and
   command-line overrides): settings, protocols, the TLS identity (in memory only) and the
   handler chain. Any failure stops here and nothing changes.
2. It binds the new listeners **while the old ones still accept**. A port that stays the same
   is never without a listener:
   - **Cleartext on BSD sockets** (the default `transport`): the new socket binds the same
     port with `SO_REUSEPORT`, which the old socket turns on only for the moment of the swap
     (another program binding the port still gets "address already in use"). The kernel sends
     new connections to the new socket; connections already queued on the old one are served,
     then it closes.
   - **HTTPS and HTTP/3** (Network.framework, which cannot share a port), and cleartext with
     `"transport": "nw"`: the running listener is handed to the new configuration as it is,
     when its address and ALPN stay the same. Its certificate comes from the same identity
     store, so a changed identity file applies to new handshakes as on a reload. Turning
     `http2` on or off changes the HTTPS listener's ALPN: that listener closes and rebinds,
     a gap of a few milliseconds on the HTTPS port only.
   - **A changed port** (`port`, `tls.port`, `http3.port`, or `host`): the new port opens; the
     old one stops accepting and closes once the swap is done.
   - A port of `0` that was `0` before keeps the port it was given.
3. The new listeners start accepting with the new settings (limits, timeouts, `maxBodySize`,
   protocols, chain).
4. The old listeners stop accepting. Their connections go on for a second (so a connection
   accepted just before the swap gets its first request answered), then drain as on SIGTERM:
   HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send `GOAWAY`, HTTP/1.1 closes idle keep-alive connections and finishes
   the request in flight with `connection: close`, tunnels end; whatever is still open after
   the new `drainTimeout` is cancelled. While the old connections drain, each set has its own
   `maxConnections`.

If a new listener cannot bind (its port is taken, a bad `host`), the listeners already bound
for the restart close and **the old ones keep serving**: stderr and `photon restart`
say `restart failed, the running server keeps serving: listener http on 127.0.0.1:8081:
Address already in use (errno 48)`, and the status file records `"result": "failed"` with
`"trigger": "restart"`. Success prints `restarted; listening …` on stderr (not stdout: the
`listening` lines there are the startup ones) and records `"result": "restarted"`.

Restarts and reloads run one at a time on the same task. A server started without `http3`
can turn it on by a restart, but its responses only advertise it (`Alt-Svc`) after a process
restart. A client that keeps a connection idle across the swap may see it closed (as on any
server closing idle keep-alive connections); HTTP clients retry such requests on a new
connection.


## A public server checklist

- Release build, installed at a stable path; firewall decision made for that path.
- `"host": "0.0.0.0"`, `port` 80, `tls.port` 443, `http3` on (UDP 443 open).
- `passwordEnv` rather than an inline `password`; `.p12` mode `0600`.
- `accessLog` to a file, rotated (move it, then SIGHUP); `metrics` behind `auth` or off.
- `maxConnections`, `maxBodySize` and `timeouts` sized for your traffic; the defaults are
  conservative.
- LaunchAgent (or LaunchDaemon) with `ExitTimeOut` above `drainTimeout`; renewal hook sends SIGHUP.
- More for proxied apps: [production checklist](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/dynamic-sites.md#production-checklist).


---

<!-- Source: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/static-sites.md (HTML: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/static-sites.html) -->

# Static websites

A static site needs only the executable and a directory:

```bash
photon serve ~/Sites/example          # http://127.0.0.1:8080/, index.html for every directory
```

(see [Serve a folder](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#serve-a-folder)), or a config file next to the site
for compression, caching, error pages and logs:

```json
{
  "root": "public",
  "compression": true,
  "caching": { "maxAge": 600 },
  "errorPages": { "404": "errors/404.html" },
  "accessLog": { "path": "logs/access.log", "format": "combined" }
}
```

Every key is in the [config reference](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#http-configjson-reference). This
page explains what the static components do.

## StaticFiles

- **Paths.** The request path is percent-decoded once (only when it contains `%`). NUL, `\`,
  an encoded `/` or a bad escape answers `400`; a `..` component answers `403`. The decoded
  path is canonicalized with `realpath`; a symlink whose target leaves the root answers `403`
  (`SymlinkPolicy.followWithinRoot`, the default; `.deny` and `.followAnywhere` are available
  from Swift).
- **Blocked names.** Components in `blockList` and, with `blockDotfiles`, any component
  starting with `.` answer `403`, case-insensitively, in the requested and the resolved path.
  `.well-known` is always allowed (ACME challenges, `security.txt`).
- **Directories.** A directory without a trailing `/` gets `301` to add it; with one, the
  first existing `index` file is served. There are no directory listings.
- **Methods.** `GET` and `HEAD`. Anything else gets `405` with `Allow: GET, HEAD` (when
  StaticFiles is the terminal handler; in the middle of a chain it passes other methods on).
- **Types.** A built-in extension table, then `mimeTypes` overrides, else `defaultMimeType`.
- **Serving.** Files up to 64 KiB are read once into an in-memory cache with their headers
  pre-rendered (up to 1024 entries); larger files are sent from an open descriptor with
  `sendfile(2)` and never read into memory (a 1 GiB download keeps the server at about 8 MiB).
  Cached entries are re-checked with `realpath` + `stat` at most once a second, so edits show
  up within a second without a restart.

## Caching and conditional requests

- Every file response carries a strong `ETag` built from size, modification time and inode
  (no content hashing), `Last-Modified`, `Accept-Ranges: bytes`, and, with `caching`,
  `Cache-Control: public, max-age=N` (default 3600 from the config file).
- Conditional requests are evaluated in RFC 9110 order: `If-Match`, `If-Unmodified-Since`,
  `If-None-Match` (lists and `*`), `If-Modified-Since`, then `If-Range`. A match answers `304`
  (with `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Cache-Control`, no body); a failed `If-Match` or
  `If-Unmodified-Since` answers `412`. Dates compare in whole seconds.
- Deploying with a tool that preserves modification times (`rsync -a`) keeps ETags stable;
  one that rewrites every file changes them all (clients then re-download once).

```bash
curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:8080/ | grep -i etag                     # ETag: "a9c-…"
curl -sI -H 'If-None-Match: "a9c-…"' http://127.0.0.1:8080/         # HTTP/1.1 304
```

## Range requests

A single `Range: bytes=…` answers `206 Partial Content` with `Content-Range`; an
unsatisfiable range answers `416`. Several ranges in one request are ignored (full `200`).
`If-Range` with a validator that no longer matches serves the whole file. This is what video
seeking and resumed downloads need.

```bash
curl -s -r 0-99 -o part http://127.0.0.1:8080/video.mp4 -w '%{http_code}\n'    # 206
```

## Error pages

`errorPages` gives bodiless `4xx`/`5xx` responses an HTML body: a small generated page by
default (`<h1>404 Not Found</h1>`), or your own files:

```json
{ "errorPages": { "404": "errors/404.html", "500": "errors/500.html" } }
```

- Paths are relative to `root` and must stay inside it; they are read once at startup (a
  missing file stops startup with a message naming `errorPages.404`).
- Statuses without a file keep the generated page; `"errorPages": false` sends empty bodies.
- `HEAD` responses, `304`, and responses that already have a body (an upstream app's own
  error JSON, for example) are never touched. The status and fields (such as `Allow` on `405`)
  are kept.
- Error pages sit outside auth and the proxy, so a `401`, `502` or `504` gets a page too.
- With `hosts`, each site looks for the file in its own root first, then in the top-level
  `root`, so every site can have its own `errors/404.html` and share the rest. A file in
  neither stops startup. The top-level `root` need not exist when the sites have the files;
  a response no site answers (`421` for an unknown host) uses the top-level file if there is
  one, else the generated page.

## Compression

`"compression": true` turns on Brotli, gzip and deflate, negotiated from `Accept-Encoding`
(q-values; `br` > `gzip` > `deflate` at equal weight), with `Vary: Accept-Encoding`.

- **Static files are compressed once.** Small files of a compressible type and at least
  `minimumSize` bytes get `br` and `gzip` variants built when they enter the file cache, at
  `precompressionLevel` (9). A request then costs no compression.
- **Sidecars.** `style.css.br` and `style.css.gz` next to `style.css` (and at least as new)
  are served as its variants, at any size. Generate them at deploy time with
  `brotli -k` / `gzip -k -9`.
- **Everything else** of a listed type (large files without sidecars, error pages, proxied
  responses) is compressed per response at `level` (4), streamed in chunks for large bodies.
- Never compressed: bodies under `minimumSize` (1024 bytes), `206`, `304`, `HEAD`, responses
  that already have `Content-Encoding`, and types outside `mimeTypes` (images, video, archives
  and `woff2` are already compressed).
- Each variant has its own strong `ETag` (`"…-br"`, `"…-gz"`), so caches and conditional
  requests stay correct.

## Virtual hosts

Several sites on one listener, chosen by `Host` (HTTP/1.1) or `:authority` (HTTP/2, HTTP/3):

```json
{
  "hosts": [
    { "names": ["example.com", "www.example.com"], "root": "sites/example" },
    { "names": ["*.blog.example.com", "blog.example.com"], "root": "sites/blog",
      "proxy": [{ "path": "/api", "upstream": "http://127.0.0.1:9000" }] },
    { "default": true, "root": "sites/fallback" }
  ]
}
```

| Key | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `hosts[].names` | array of strings | Host names, matched without the port, case-insensitively. `*.a.test` matches any subdomain of `a.test` (not `a.test` itself) |
| `hosts[].name` | string | One name (alternative to `names`) |
| `hosts[].root` | string (required) | The site's directory, relative to the config file |
| `hosts[].default` | bool | This site answers unknown hosts and requests without a host. At most one |
| `hosts[].proxy` | array | Proxy mounts for this site only, tried before the top-level `proxy` mounts |

- A request for an unknown host goes to the `default` site, or gets `421 Misdirected Request`
  without one.
- With `hosts`, the top-level `root` is not served and need not exist; the other file keys
  (`index`, `mimeTypes`, `blockList`, `caching`, `compression`, `errorPages`) apply to every
  site. `errorPages` files resolve per site (see [Error pages](#error-pages)).
- With TLS, all names are served with the one identity in `tls.identity`, so use a certificate
  that covers every name (SAN or wildcard). There is no per-host certificate (SNI) selection.

## Authentication

`auth` protects path prefixes with HTTP Basic, JWT bearer tokens or static bearer tokens:

```json
{
  "auth": [
    { "paths": ["/admin"], "realm": "Admin", "basic": { "file": "users.htpasswd" } },
    { "paths": ["/api/private"], "realm": "API",
      "jwt": { "keys": [{ "id": "k1", "secretEnv": "JWT_KEY" }], "issuer": "https://id.example.com", "audience": "api" },
      "tokens": [{ "name": "ci", "sha256": "9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08" }] }
  ]
}
```

| Key | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `paths` | string or array | Path prefixes starting with `/`. The first area covering a path decides |
| `realm` | string | Shown in the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge |
| `basic` | string or object | A credential file name, or `{"file", "users", "usersEnv"}`: lines `user:$pbkdf2-sha256$…` from a file, inline, or an environment variable. Plaintext passwords are refused |
| `jwt.keys` | array | `{"id"?, "secret" \| "secretEnv"}`; HS256 secrets of at least 32 bytes |
| `jwt.issuer`, `jwt.audience` | string; string or array | Required `iss` / `aud` when set |
| `jwt.leeway` | integer 0–3600 | Clock skew allowed, seconds |
| `jwt.requireExp` | bool | Default `true`: tokens need `exp` |
| `tokens` | array | Static bearer tokens as `{"name", "sha256"}` (hex SHA-256 of the token; the token itself is never stored) |

An area needs at least one of `basic`, `jwt` or `tokens`.

Make a Basic credential line (PBKDF2-SHA256, 600,000 iterations by default):

```bash
scripts/hash-password.sh alice >> users.htpasswd      # prompts for the password
```

Make a token digest: `printf %s "$TOKEN" | shasum -a 256`.

Behaviour: missing or wrong credentials get `401` with one challenge per accepted scheme;
passwords are compared in constant time; a client address with 10 failures within 60 seconds
gets `429` with `Retry-After` before any hashing; requests outside every area pass after one
prefix check. Credentials are never logged. Basic sends the password with every request, so
use it only over HTTPS. Auth runs before the proxy, so it also protects proxied paths; the
upstream receives the `Authorization` header unchanged.


---

<!-- Source: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/dynamic-sites.md (HTML: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/dynamic-sites.html) -->

# Dynamic websites

Two ways to serve dynamic content:

| | In-process Swift | Reverse proxy |
|---|---|---|
| What | Your handlers run inside the server: `Router` routes, `WebSocketUpgrade` endpoints, any `HTTPHandler` | The server forwards path prefixes to apps on localhost (Go, Node, Python, Rails, another Swift server…) over HTTP/1.1 or a Unix socket |
| Build | Your own Swift package composing PhotonHTTP's products | The shipped executable plus a `proxy` key; no Swift code |
| Cost per request | A function call | Two loopback round trips (about 18 µs added, see [performance](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/performance.md)) |
| Good for | APIs and real-time endpoints written in Swift | Existing apps in any language; isolating an app in its own process |

Both mix freely with static files: static at `/`, dynamic under `/api`.

## In-process with Router

```swift
let router = try Router {
    GET("/api/users/:id") { request, context in
        guard let id = context.params.decimal("id") else { return HTTPResponse(status: .badRequest) }
        return json(#"{"id": \#(id)}"#)
    }
    POST("/api/users") { request, _ in
        let body = try await request.body.collect(upTo: 64 * 1024)   // bounded; 413-style limit is yours
        …
    }
    Group("/api/admin") {
        GET("/stats") { _, _ in … }
        Route("/files/*path", methods: [.get, .put]) { _, context in
            let path = context.params["path"] ?? ""
            …
        }
    }
}
let server = Server(listeners: [listener], protocols: [HTTP1()]) {
    router              // misses fall through to the files
    files
}
```

A complete, runnable version (with `json(_:)` and signal handling) is
[`Examples/custom-server`](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Examples/custom-server/README.md), walked through in
[Choosing components](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md#a-custom-server-package).

Router rules:

- Patterns: literal segments, `:name` captures one non-empty segment, a trailing `*` or
  `*name` captures the rest. Literals compare with the still-encoded path; captures are
  percent-decoded when read (`context.params["id"]`, `.decimal("id")`, `.wildcard`).
- At each segment a literal beats a parameter beats a wildcard, with backtracking.
- A `GET` route also answers `HEAD` unless a `HEAD` route exists.
- A path that matches with a method no route answers gets `405` with `Allow`. Anything else
  falls through to the next element (as a middleware) or gets `404` (as a handler).
- Two routes matching the same paths with the same method are rejected when the router is
  built (`RouterError`).
- Matching allocates nothing; reading a capture as `String` allocates.

Handler rules (the request-path contract):

- An `HTTPRequest` is valid only during the call. Copy what you keep (`request.snapshot()`,
  `request.string(of: request.path)`), never store the request.
- Read bodies with a limit: `try await request.body.collect(upTo:)`, or iterate
  `request.body` (an `AsyncSequence` of `ByteBuffer`) to stream. The server already enforces
  `maxBodySize`.
- Stream large or slow responses with `.stream(length:writer:)`: each `write` waits for the
  client (backpressure), so memory stays bounded. `.file(FileRegion)` sends a file with
  `sendfile`.
- Do not block the cooperative thread pool (no synchronous network calls, `sleep`, or long CPU
  loops in a handler); offload long CPU work to your own executor or process.
- Shared mutable state: a `Mutex` (Synchronization) with short, non-suspending critical
  sections. An actor works, but every request then hops to it.
- Protect routes with `Authenticator` in front of the router, or per route with
  `GET("/me", handler: auth.protect(MeHandler()))`; the principal is `context.principal`.

## WebSockets

```swift
let chat = WebSocketUpgrade(path: "/ws",
                            origin: { $0.origin == "https://example.com" },  // stop cross-site use
                            subprotocol: { $0.offeredSubprotocols.first }) { socket, request in
    for await message in socket.messages {
        switch message {
        case .text(let text): try await socket.send(text: "echo: \(text)")
        case .binary: try await socket.send(message)
        }
    }
}
let server = Server(listeners: listeners, protocols: [HTTP2(configuration: h2), HTTP1()]) {
    chat
    router
    files
}
```

- One component serves RFC 6455 on HTTP/1.1, RFC 8441 extended CONNECT on HTTP/2 and RFC 9220
  on HTTP/3; HTTP/2 advertises extended CONNECT automatically when a `WebSocketUpgrade` is in
  the chain.
- `socket.messages` is an `AsyncSequence` of `.text(String)` (validated UTF-8) or
  `.binary(ByteBuffer)`; the inbound queue is bounded, so a slow consumer applies backpressure.
- permessage-deflate is negotiated when `WebSocketConfiguration.compression` is set.
- On server shutdown the session closes with 1001 (going away).
- The shipped executable has no in-process WebSockets; it can only *proxy* them
  (`"websocket": true` on a mount).

## Reverse proxy to localhost apps

The executable forwards mounted path prefixes to upstream HTTP/1.1 apps and serves everything
else from files. Example with the Go app in [`Examples/go-api`](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Examples/go-api/main.go)
(stdlib only; `GET /api/health`, CRUD on `/api/items`, `GET /api/echo` shows the forwarded
headers):

```json
{
  "root": "Public",
  "proxy": [
    { "path": "/api", "upstream": "http://127.0.0.1:9000",
      "timeouts": { "connect": 2, "response": 30 } }
  ]
}
```

```bash
(cd Examples/go-api && go run . -addr 127.0.0.1:9000) &
.build/release/photon --config Root/http-config.proxy.json   # needs scripts/make-test-identity.sh (TLS)
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/health        # {"status":"ok"}
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/echo          # shows X-Forwarded-For/Proto/Host/Prefix
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/                  # Root/Public/index.html
```

How requests flow:

- Mounts match by path prefix on segment boundaries, longest first (`/api` matches `/api` and
  `/api/x`, not `/apix`). Paths are normalized first, so `/%61pi` and `/x/../api` match `/api`.
  In a `hosts` site, its own mounts are tried first, then the top-level ones, then its files.
- The proxy sits after `auth` and before the files: protected prefixes are checked before
  anything is forwarded, and `errorPages` renders `502`/`504`.
- Requests from HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 clients all go upstream as HTTP/1.1, over pooled
  keep-alive connections. Hop-by-hop fields are removed. Response bodies stream through.
- A refused or failed connection, or a malformed response, is `502 Bad Gateway`; no response
  head within `timeouts.response` is `504 Gateway Timeout`. A failure after the head aborts the
  response (close on HTTP/1.1, stream reset on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3).
- After a connect failure, `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS` and `TRACE` are retried on
  the next upstream (`retries`, default 1); `POST` and `PATCH` never are.
- A client that goes away cancels the upstream request.
- `Expect: 100-continue` is answered by the server itself; `1xx` from upstream are consumed.
- WebSocket and other `Upgrade` requests are tunnelled with `"websocket": true` (h1 Upgrade,
  h2/h3 extended CONNECT become an h1 Upgrade upstream).
- Upstreams are `http://HOST:PORT[/base]` or `unix:/path/to.sock`. **`https://` upstreams are
  not supported.**

### Proxy mount reference

`proxy` is an array of mounts (a single object is accepted). The same `path` twice for
overlapping hosts is an error.

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | string | `"/"` | Prefix starting with `/` |
| `host` / `hosts` | string / array | all hosts | Only for these `Host` names (one of the two) |
| `upstream` / `upstreams` | string / array (required) | – | `http://HOST:PORT[/base]` or `unix:/path`. Several upstreams are used round-robin, skipping unhealthy ones (one of the two) |
| `stripPrefix` | bool | `false` | Remove the mount path before forwarding (`/api/x` → `/x`) |
| `preserveHost` | bool | `false` | Send the client's `Host` instead of the upstream's |
| `forwardedHeaders` | string | `"x-forwarded"` | `x-forwarded` (`X-Forwarded-For/Proto/Host/Prefix`), `forwarded` (RFC 7239), `both`, `none` |
| `trustedProxies` | array | `[]` | IPs or CIDR ranges (`"10.0.0.0/8"`, `"::1"`) whose forwarded fields are kept and appended to; from anyone else they are replaced |
| `rewriteLocation` | bool | `true` | Rewrite upstream `Location` and `Content-Location` into the client's URL space |
| `rewriteCookiePath` | bool | `false` | With `stripPrefix` or a base path, rewrite `Set-Cookie` `Path` (`Path=/` → `Path=/api`) |
| `websocket` | bool | `false` | Tunnel WebSocket / `Upgrade` requests |
| `timeouts.connect` | seconds, `0`/`null` off | `10` | Connecting to the upstream |
| `timeouts.response` | seconds, `0`/`null` off | `60` | Request sent → response head |
| `timeouts.idle` | seconds, `0`/`null` off | `60` | Between body reads; also closes an idle tunnel (tunnels default to 300 s without it) |
| `timeouts.total` | seconds, `0`/`null` off | none | Whole exchange |
| `retries` | integer 0–10 | `1` | Extra attempts on the next upstream after a connect failure, idempotent methods only |
| `health.failures` | integer 0–1000 | `3` | Consecutive failures that mark an upstream down (`0`: passive tracking off) |
| `health.cooldown` | seconds | `10` | How long it stays down |
| `health.path` | string | none | Active check: `GET path` every `interval`; status < 500 is healthy |
| `health.interval` | seconds > 0 | `10` | Active check period |
| `pool.maxConnections` | integer | `0` (no limit) | Connections per upstream; more requests queue |
| `pool.queue` | integer | `256` | Requests that may wait for a connection; a full queue gets `503` |
| `pool.queueTimeout` | seconds > 0 | `10` | Longest wait in the queue (`503` after) |
| `pool.maxIdle` | integer | `16` | Kept-alive idle connections per upstream. **Raise it to your expected concurrency**: with more concurrent requests than `maxIdle`, extra connections are opened and closed per request |
| `pool.idleTimeout` | seconds | `60` | Idle connections closed after this (`0` keeps them) |

For all four `timeouts` keys, `0` or `null` turns that limit off and a missing key keeps the
default (`total` is off by default). Values are capped at one year. For long-polling or
streaming upstreams (server-sent events, long downloads), set `"idle": 0` and `"response": 0`
(or large values); `idle: 0` also leaves upgraded tunnels without an idle limit.

### Apache `mod_proxy` → PhotonHTTP

| Apache | `proxy` mount |
|---|---|
| `ProxyPass /api http://127.0.0.1:9000/api` | `{"path": "/api", "upstream": "http://127.0.0.1:9000"}` |
| `ProxyPass /api/ http://127.0.0.1:9000/` | `{"path": "/api", "upstream": "http://127.0.0.1:9000", "stripPrefix": true}` |
| `ProxyPass /app http://127.0.0.1:9000/v2` | `{"path": "/app", "upstream": "http://127.0.0.1:9000/v2", "stripPrefix": true}` |
| `ProxyPassReverse` | `"rewriteLocation": true` (default) |
| `ProxyPassReverseCookiePath` | `"rewriteCookiePath": true` |
| `ProxyPreserveHost On` | `"preserveHost": true` |
| `RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto …` | automatic with `"forwardedHeaders": "x-forwarded"` (default) |
| `RemoteIPTrustedProxy` | `"trustedProxies": ["10.0.0.0/8"]` |
| `<Proxy balancer://…>` + `BalancerMember` | `"upstreams": [ … ]` (round-robin, unhealthy members skipped) |
| `ProxyTimeout`, `connectiontimeout=`, `timeout=` | `"timeouts": {"connect": …, "response": …, "idle": …}` |
| `retry=` on a worker | `"health": {"cooldown": …}` |
| `max=` on a worker | `"pool": {"maxConnections": …}` |
| `ProxyPass /ws ws://…` (`mod_proxy_wstunnel`) | `"websocket": true` |
| `ProxyPass … unix:/path.sock\|http://localhost/` | `"upstream": "unix:/path.sock"` |
| `ProxyPass` inside a `<VirtualHost>` | `hosts[].proxy`, or `"host"`/`"hosts"` on a top-level mount |
| `<Location /admin>` + `AuthType Basic` | `"auth": [{"paths": ["/admin"], "basic": …}]` |
| `ProxyPass` to `https://` | not supported: run the app on HTTP on localhost or a Unix socket |

## System 1 decision server (Laya)

[laya-go](https://github.com/brennanMKE/laya-go)'s `laya-server` runs Laya, a System 1 decision
model, on the Mac's GPU with Metal and serves `POST /predict` (`{"state": …, "questions": {…}}`
→ `{"answers": {…}}`, or a `"batch"` of states), `GET /health` and `GET /stats`. It has no
authentication, so keep it on loopback (`--host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000`) and put it behind a
proxy mount, with the prefix stripped so `/laya/predict` reaches `/predict`:

```json
{
  "root": "public",
  "proxy": [
    { "path": "/laya", "upstream": "http://127.0.0.1:8000", "stripPrefix": true,
      "timeouts": { "connect": 2, "response": 60 },
      "pool": { "maxIdle": 8 } }
  ],
  "auth": [ { "paths": ["/laya"], "tokens": [{ "name": "game", "sha256": "…" }] } ]
}
```

laya-server loads the model before it starts listening, so a request during its startup gets a
fast `502`, not a hang. A deployment that serves a game from one Mac and asks a laya-server on
another over Tailscale is in
[`Examples/parallax-gordon/README.md`](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Examples/parallax-gordon/README.md).

### In-process with LayaKit (when it can answer)

> **Not runnable yet.** [LayaKit](https://github.com/brennanMKE/laya-swift), the Swift + Metal
> port of laya-go, is bootstrapped: it compiles the Metal shaders and loads the fixtures, but its
> `LayaModel` is a placeholder that cannot answer questions. The sketch below uses the API
> planned in laya-swift's `docs/swift-port.md` (`LayaModel.load`, `predict`, `LayaState`,
> `NamedQuestion`), which may change. LayaKit is **not** a dependency of PhotonHTTP; it
> would be a dependency of your own server package.

Design:

- **One shared model**, loaded once at startup (weights and Metal pipelines take time and about
  1 GB), before the listeners bind, and captured by the route closure.
- **GPU calls are serialized by the model, not by the server.** `LayaModel` is an `actor` and
  its Metal engine runs one pass at a time on its own serial executor (the GPU is saturated by
  one pass anyway). A handler simply `await`s it. That is one actor hop per prediction, which is
  acceptable here because a forward pass costs milliseconds; the server's own request path
  stays actor-free.
- **Bounded admission.** Requests queue on the actor without limit, so the handler keeps an
  in-flight count in a `Mutex` (a non-suspending check-and-increment) and answers `503` when it
  is full, instead of letting latency grow.
- **Batching** comes from the request: a `batch` body maps to one `predictMany` call (one
  forward pass). An answer cache keyed by (state, question) can sit in front, as in laya-go.
- Decoding the JSON body with Foundation is fine here: it is application code, and the pass
  dwarfs it.

```swift
import Foundation
import HTTPCore
import LayaKit          // your package's dependency, not PhotonHTTP's
import Router
import Synchronization

/// Admission control: at most `limit` predictions in flight; the rest get 503.
final class Gate: Sendable {
    private let inFlight = Mutex(0)
    let limit: Int
    init(limit: Int) { self.limit = limit }
    func enter() -> Bool { inFlight.withLock { n in guard n < limit else { return false }; n += 1; return true } }
    func leave() { inFlight.withLock { $0 -= 1 } }
}

let model = try await LayaModel.load(LayaOptions())      // once, before the server starts
let gate = Gate(limit: 32)

let laya = try Router {
    POST("/laya/predict") { request, _ in
        guard gate.enter() else { return HTTPResponse(status: .serviceUnavailable) }
        defer { gate.leave() }
        let body = try await request.body.collect(upTo: 1 << 20)
        let (state, questions) = try decodePredictRequest(body)   // your JSON → LayaState, [NamedQuestion]
        let result = try await model.predict(state, questions)    // hops to the actor; one GPU pass
        return json(encodeAnswers(result))                        // laya-go's wire format
    }
    GET("/laya/health") { _, _ in json(#"{"ok": true}"#) }
}
// Server(…) { laya; files } as in Examples/custom-server.
```

Until LayaKit answers, use the reverse-proxy setup above: the HTTP contract is the same, so a
client does not change when the model moves in-process.

## Production checklist

- **Upstreams on loopback or Unix sockets only.** Bind apps to `127.0.0.1` (or a socket) so
  the only way in is through PhotonHTTP, its auth and its logs.
- **Pool sizing.** Set `pool.maxIdle` to the concurrency you expect per upstream (the M17
  benchmark ran out of loopback ports with the default 16 at 64 concurrent clients before
  `maxIdle` was raised), and `pool.maxConnections` to what the app can handle.
- **Timeouts.** `connect` short (1–2 s on loopback), `response` just above your slowest
  endpoint, `total` for endpoints that must never hang; `idle` for streaming responses.
- **Health.** Several upstreams with `health.path` for active checks; `retries` only helps
  idempotent requests.
- **Forwarded headers.** Leave `x-forwarded` on so apps see the client address and scheme;
  set `trustedProxies` only for a load balancer you run in front.
- **Cookies and redirects.** With `stripPrefix`, keep `rewriteLocation` on and turn on
  `rewriteCookiePath` if the app sets `Path=/`.
- **Body limits.** `maxBodySize` (and `http2.maxRequestBodySize`) bound uploads before the app
  sees them.
- **Auth at the edge.** `auth` areas on admin and private API prefixes; HTTPS for anything
  with credentials.
- **Logging.** `accessLog` records proxied statuses (`502`/`504` included); watch for them.
- **Process supervision.** Run each app and the server under launchd (see
  [LaunchAgents](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#running-as-a-launchagent)); the server starts fine before
  its upstreams and answers `502` until they are up.
- **Restarts.** There is no config reload: changing mounts means a restart, which drains
  in-flight requests first.


---

<!-- Source: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/tls.md (HTML: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/tls.html) -->

# TLS

How PhotonHTTP does TLS: where the handshake runs, what identity formats it loads, how
ALPN picks HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, what you can and cannot tune, how to get and test a
certificate without touching the keychain, and what the identity errors mean. The config keys
and the short HTTPS recipe are in [Running on a Mac](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#https-with-a-pkcs12-identity);
this guide goes deeper and links there rather than repeating it.

## How TLS is done

TLS runs entirely inside Network.framework; there is no TLS code of our own.

```
PKCS#12 file ─▶ TLSIdentity (SecPKCS12Import, memory only) ─┬─▶ TLSConfiguration ─▶ TCPListener (TLS over TCP: h2, http/1.1)
                                                             └─▶ QUICListener (TLS 1.3 inside QUIC: h3)
```

| Type | File | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `TLSIdentity` | [TLSIdentity.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/NetworkTransport/TLSIdentity.swift) | Certificate and private key imported from PKCS#12 in memory; `certificateDER` is the leaf |
| `TLSIdentityError` | same | `fileUnreadable(path:)`, `importFailed(status:)`, `noIdentity`, `unsupportedKeyType`, `notUsableForTLS`; the description says what to check |
| `TLSIdentityStore` | same | The identity listeners present, replaceable while they run (`replace(with:)`, used by SIGHUP) |
| `TLSConfiguration` | [TLSConfiguration.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/NetworkTransport/TLSConfiguration.swift) | Server TLS settings for a `TCPListener`: identity (or `identityStore`), version range, ALPN, client certificates, handshake timeout |
| `TLSConfigurationError` | same | An unsupported minimum or maximum TLS version, or an empty range |
| `TLSClientConfiguration` | same | Client settings for `TCPTransport.connect(…, tls:)`, used by tests and tools (ALPN, pinned certificate, SNI, versions) |
| `TCPListener` | [TCPListener.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/NetworkTransport/TCPListener.swift) | `TCPListener(configuration:tls:)`: Network.framework TCP with `NWProtocolTLS` |
| `QUICListener` | [QUICListener.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/NetworkTransport/QUICListener.swift) | `QUICListener(configuration:identity:)` or `(configuration:identityStore:)`: QUIC with the same identity |
| `ConnectionInfo` | [Transport.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTPCore/Transport.swift) | `isSecure`, `negotiatedALPN`, `tlsVersion` of each connection, visible to handlers as `context.connection` |
| `TLSNegotiated` | [TLSNegotiated.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTPServer/TLSNegotiated.swift) | Runs HTTP/2 when ALPN chose `h2`, HTTP/1.1 otherwise |

Points that follow from this design:

- **Two listeners can use TLS**: `TCPListener` with a `TLSConfiguration` (HTTPS: HTTP/1.1 and
  HTTP/2) and `QUICListener` (HTTP/3). The BSD-socket listener (`BSDSocketListener`, the
  default cleartext transport) has no TLS. `"transport": "nw"` changes only the cleartext
  listener; HTTPS is always Network.framework.
- **Handshake first, then hand-over.** An accepted TLS connection is handed to the server only
  after its handshake is done, so the negotiated ALPN token and TLS version are final when the
  protocol is chosen. A connection whose handshake fails (cleartext on the TLS port, an ALPN
  offer the server does not accept, a rejected certificate) is closed, logged under the
  `PhotonHTTP` subsystem, category `TLS`, and counted in `TCPListener.failedHandshakeCount`.
  It never reaches the handler.
- **Handshake timeout.** A connection that does not finish the TCP and TLS handshakes within
  `TLSConfiguration.handshakeTimeout` (default 10 s) is reset, so silent clients cannot hold
  the listener's pending-connection slots (`pendingConnectionLimit`, default 64). The executable
  uses the default; it has no config key.
- **No half-close over TLS.** Network.framework sends neither `close_notify` nor a FIN for a
  final-message send on TLS; both go out only when the connection is closed (#0118). Clients
  see the response end normally; only code that relies on a TLS half-close notices.

### No keychain, ever

`TLSIdentity` always calls `SecPKCS12Import` with `kSecImportToMemoryOnly: true`. Without that
option macOS adds the private key to the login keychain, and the first TLS signature then blocks
