on a SecurityAgent prompt: the handshake simply hangs. Nothing in the server reads, adds or
changes keychain items or certificate trust settings. Test clients accept the test certificate
by pinning its DER bytes in a verify block (`TLSClientConfiguration.pinnedCertificate`,
`QUICPeerVerification.pinnedCertificate`), again without the keychain. The same rules apply to
anything you add: see [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/AGENTS.md).

### Identity format and password

- **PKCS#12 only.** The identity is one `.p12` file with the private key and the certificate
  chain (leaf first, then intermediates). PEM certificate and key files are not loaded directly;
  convert them (see [Converting PEM to PKCS#12](#converting-pem-to-pkcs12)). The first identity
  in the bundle is used.
- **One identity per server.** The executable loads it at startup and gives the same
  `TLSIdentityStore` to the HTTPS and the HTTP/3 listener; SIGHUP rereads the file and swaps
  the identity in that store (see **Reload** below).
- **Password**: `tls.password` (inline) or `tls.passwordEnv` (the name of an environment
  variable), exactly one of the two. An unset variable stops startup with
  `"tls.passwordEnv": environment variable NAME is not set`. Prefer `passwordEnv` and keep the
  `.p12` at mode `0600`.
- **Paths** are relative to the directory holding the config file
  ([`Root/http-config.tls.json`](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Root/http-config.tls.json) points at
  `../.test-identity/server.p12`).

## ALPN and protocol selection

ALPN ([RFC 7301](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7301)) lets the client and server agree on
the application protocol inside the TLS handshake, so no bytes are sniffed on TLS.

**What the server offers.** A listener's ALPN list is not configured by hand. When `Server`
binds a listener created with the `make` form (`.byteStream(name:) { bind in … }`), it passes
`bind.alpnTokens`:

- for a byte-stream (TCP/TLS) listener, the protocol registry's tokens in registration
  (preference) order: `TLSNegotiated(HTTP2(), fallback: HTTP1())` gives `["h2", "http/1.1"]`,
  `[HTTP1()]` alone gives `["http/1.1"]`;
- for a multiplexed (QUIC) listener, its protocol's own tokens: `HTTP3` gives `["h3"]`.

So the TLS listener offers exactly what the server can speak. Network.framework fixes the TLS
options when the listener is created, which is why the listener is built at bind time.

**What a connection runs** ([ProtocolRegistry.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTPServer/ProtocolRegistry.swift)):

| Client offers | Negotiated | Executable default (`TLSNegotiated(HTTP2(), fallback: HTTP1())`) |
|---|---|---|
| `h2, http/1.1` (browsers, curl) | `h2` | HTTP/2 |
| `http/1.1` (`curl --http1.1`) | `http/1.1` | HTTP/1.1 |
| no ALPN | none (`negotiatedALPN == nil`) | HTTP/1.1, the TLS default |
| only tokens the server does not accept | handshake fails with a `no_application_protocol` alert | nothing; counted as a failed handshake |
| cleartext bytes on the TLS port | handshake fails | nothing |

With `"http2": false` the server registers only HTTP/1.1 and offers only `http/1.1`; a client
that offers only `h2` then fails the handshake.

### `TLSNegotiated`

`TLSNegotiated<Preferred, Fallback>` (HTTPServer, public since #0130) is one
`ConnectionProtocol` that runs `Preferred` when the connection is TLS and negotiated one of
`Preferred.alpnTokens`, and `Fallback` for everything else: `http/1.1`, no ALPN, and cleartext.
Its `alpnTokens` are `Preferred`'s followed by `Fallback`'s without duplicates.

Because it is the only registered protocol, cleartext connections are neither sniffed nor
wrapped in a replay transport: the cleartext port costs exactly what HTTP/1.1 alone costs. This
is what the executable registers unless `"http2": {"cleartext": true}`, in which case it
registers `[HTTP2(), HTTP1()]` and sniffs every cleartext connection for the HTTP/2 preface
(h2c prior knowledge). HTTP/2 over TLS is selected by ALPN only, as
[RFC 9113 §3.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-3.3) requires; there is no
h2c `Upgrade`.

### HTTP/3: TLS 1.3 inside QUIC

QUIC carries its own TLS 1.3 handshake ([RFC 9001](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001));
there is no TLS 1.2 for HTTP/3. `QUICListener` takes the same `TLSIdentity` (or the same
`TLSIdentityStore`, so a reload reaches both listeners) and sets only the identity and the
ALPN list (`h3`) on its security options. `TLSConfiguration`'s version range,
client certificates and handshake timeout apply to the TCP listener only.

Browsers find HTTP/3 through `Alt-Svc`. The `AltSvc` middleware (HTTP3 target) adds
`Alt-Svc: h3=":PORT"; ma=SECONDS` to responses on TLS connections that are not HTTP/3 (it
tests `isSecure && negotiatedALPN != "h3"`); cleartext responses never carry it, because a
client must not trust an alternative learned over an unauthenticated connection. The executable
registers it only when `http3` is on and sets the port once the UDP listener is bound;
`http3.altSvcMaxAge` (default 86400) is the `ma`. Details: [HTTP/3](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/http3.md#how-clients-find-it-alt-svc).

### Seeing what was negotiated

Every handler and middleware sees the connection's TLS state in `context.connection`:

```swift
struct ShowTLS: HTTPMiddleware {
    func handle<Next: HTTPHandler>(_ request: HTTPRequest, context: RequestContext,
                                   next: Next) async throws -> HTTPResponse {
        let connection = context.connection
        // isSecure: true for TLS and QUIC. negotiatedALPN: "h2", "http/1.1", "h3" or nil.
        // tlsVersion: .v1_2, .v1_3, or nil on cleartext.
        if connection.isSecure, connection.tlsVersion == .v1_2 { /* … */ }
        return try await next.handle(request, context: context)
    }
}
```

`TLSVersion` prints as `TLSv1.2` / `TLSv1.3`.

## Versions, ciphers and other knobs

| Setting | Swift (`TLSConfiguration`) | `http-config.json` |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum version | `minimumVersion`, default `.v1_2` | none: TLS 1.2 |
| Maximum version | `maximumVersion`, default `nil` (the system's highest, TLS 1.3) | none: TLS 1.3 |
| ALPN | `alpn`, default `["http/1.1"]`; pass `bind.alpnTokens` | from `http2` (`h2` on by default) |
| Client certificates | `clientAuthentication`, default `nil` | none |
| Handshake timeout | `handshakeTimeout`, default 10 s | none |

- **Versions.** Network.framework negotiates the highest version both sides support, so TLS 1.3
  is used whenever the client offers it. To require TLS 1.3 on HTTPS, set
  `minimumVersion: .v1_3` in a custom server. Only `.v1_2` and `.v1_3` are accepted: any other
  `minimumVersion` or `maximumVersion` (TLS 1.0, 1.1, an unknown value) or a minimum above the
  maximum makes `TCPListener.init` throw `TLSConfigurationError` (for example `unsupported
  minimum TLS version TLS(0x301): use TLSv1.2 or TLSv1.3`); nothing is clamped.
  `TLSConfiguration.validate()` runs the same check up front.
- **Ciphers, curves, session resumption, 0-RTT.** The server sets none of these: whatever
  Network.framework's defaults are for the macOS release applies. There is no cipher list to
  tune, and the server does not use 0-RTT (early data) on either TLS or QUIC.
- **SNI and virtual hosts.** The server does not read the SNI name and cannot pick a
  certificate per name: there is one identity. With [virtual hosts](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/static-sites.md#virtual-hosts),
  which route by `Host` / `:authority` after the handshake, the certificate must cover every
  name as a subject alternative name (one SAN certificate, or a wildcard). Requests are routed
  by `Host`, whatever SNI the client sent.
- **Client certificates (mutual TLS)** are Swift-only. `TLSConfiguration.ClientAuthentication`
  has `required` (default `true`) and a `verify` closure that receives the client's chain as DER
  (leaf first) and returns whether to accept it. It runs on a Network.framework queue during the
  handshake, so it must not block. A required certificate that is missing fails the handshake
  (with TLS 1.3 the client may see this only as the connection ending after it thinks it is
  connected). The verified chain is not passed on to handlers; `ConnectionInfo` has no
  client-certificate field.
- **Reload.** SIGHUP rereads the identity file (in memory only, like at startup), whether or
  not `tls` changed in the config, so a renewal written over the same path is picked up without
  a restart. New HTTPS and HTTP/3 handshakes present the new certificate; connections already
  open keep the one they negotiated, and no listener is closed or rebound. stderr says which
  happened: `reload: TLS identity PATH reloaded; new HTTPS and HTTP/3 handshakes use the new
  certificate`, `reload: TLS identity PATH unchanged`, or `warning: reload: cannot load TLS
  identity PATH: …; keeping the current TLS certificate` (bad file or password: the old
  certificate stays). `tls.identity` and `tls.password` / `tls.passwordEnv` may change too (a
  `passwordEnv` is read from the environment the server started with); adding or removing
  `tls`, or changing `tls.port`, still needs a restart
  ([reload table](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#shutdown-restart-and-reload)). If the config file itself
  fails to reload, the identity is not reread either.
  In a custom server, build listeners from one `TLSIdentityStore` (`TLSConfiguration(identityStore:)`,
  `QUICListener(configuration:identityStore:)`) and call `store.replace(with:)`: the listeners
  ask the store for the identity on every handshake (`sec_protocol_options_set_challenge_block`),
  because Network.framework fixes a listener's options when it is created.

### HSTS

The server does not send `Strict-Transport-Security` itself. Add it with a small middleware
that marks only TLS responses (a browser ignores the header over cleartext anyway):

```swift
import HTTPCore

struct HSTS: HTTPMiddleware {
    // StaticString: appended without building a String per response.
    static let name: StaticString = "strict-transport-security"
    static let value: StaticString = "max-age=31536000"

    func handle<Next: HTTPHandler>(_ request: HTTPRequest, context: RequestContext,
                                   next: Next) async throws -> HTTPResponse {
        var response = try await next.handle(request, context: context)
        if context.connection.isSecure {
            response.headers.append(name: Self.name, value: Self.value)
        }
        return response
    }
}
```

Put it early in the chain (before `StaticFiles` and the router). The shipped executable has no
key for it; a server built from `ConfigFile` can wrap the built chain. Turn HSTS on only once
HTTPS works for every name the site serves (and every subdomain, if you add
`includeSubDomains`): browsers remember it for `max-age` seconds. If the site is reached through a TLS-terminating proxy and
PhotonHTTP itself speaks cleartext, `isSecure` is false; send the header from the proxy.

## Getting a certificate

### The test identity

```bash
scripts/make-test-identity.sh            # creates it if missing (idempotent)
scripts/make-test-identity.sh --force    # replaces it
scripts/make-test-identity.sh --name second   # a second identity in .test-identity/second/
```

The second identity (`TestIdentity.load(name: "second")`) has its own key and certificate;
the certificate-reload tests (#0140) swap between the two.

It writes the gitignored `.test-identity/` folder at the repository root:

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `server.p12` | PKCS#12 identity, password `sws-test-password` |
| `cert.pem` | The certificate (PEM) |
| `cert.der` | The certificate (DER), for pinning in test clients |
| `key.pem` | The private key, unencrypted |

The certificate is self-signed, ECDSA P-256, valid 825 days, `CN=localhost` with SANs
`DNS:localhost`, `IP:127.0.0.1`, `IP:::1`, and `extendedKeyUsage=serverAuth`. The script only
runs `openssl` on files (Homebrew's `/opt/homebrew/bin/openssl` when installed; override with
`OPENSSL=…`). Tests call `TestIdentity.load()` (HTTPTestSupport), which runs the script when
the identity is missing. A local CA for browser testing is still open work (#0072, #0062,
#0105); until then browsers reject this certificate unless you trust it by hand.

### Let's Encrypt

See [A real certificate (Let's Encrypt)](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#a-real-certificate-lets-encrypt):
any ACME client that writes PEM files, HTTP-01 through `/.well-known/` on your site's root,
then the conversion below and a SIGHUP on renewal (write the new `.p12` over the old path).

### Tailscale

On a tailnet with HTTPS certificates enabled, `tailscale cert` fetches a Let's Encrypt
certificate for the machine's `*.ts.net` name and writes PEM files:

```bash
tailscale cert mymac.example-tailnet.ts.net
# writes mymac.example-tailnet.ts.net.crt and .key in the current directory
```

Convert them as below. `tailscale cert` depends on the Tailscale control plane and Let's
Encrypt, and it can fail; it has returned an HTTP 500 for us. Retry later, and keep the
previous `.p12` in place until a new one is made. The name is reachable only on your tailnet,
so the server can bind the Tailscale address or stay on loopback behind `tailscale serve`.

### Converting PEM to PKCS#12

```bash
export SWS_P12_PASSWORD='a long random password'
openssl pkcs12 -export \
  -inkey example.key -in example.crt \
  -out certs/example.p12 -passout env:SWS_P12_PASSWORD \
  -keypbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -certpbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -macalg sha1
chmod 600 certs/example.p12
```

- `-in` must be the full chain, leaf first. If the intermediates are in a separate file, add
  `-certfile chain.pem`.
- The legacy algorithms matter: `SecPKCS12Import` does not reliably accept OpenSSL 3's default
  AES-256/PBKDF2 encryption, and fails with an import error (see
  [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)). The test-identity script uses the same flags.
- This only writes a file. Do not double-click the `.p12` or import it with Keychain Access:
  the server does not need it in a keychain, and importing it is exactly what the server avoids.

Check a bundle without the server:

```bash
openssl pkcs12 -info -in certs/example.p12 -passin env:SWS_P12_PASSWORD -nokeys | openssl x509 -noout -subject -ext subjectAltName -enddate
```

## Testing safely

Start the server on loopback (as `Root/http-config.tls.json` does) and test with clients that
accept the certificate per command, never by trusting it system-wide:

```bash
scripts/make-test-identity.sh
.build/release/photon --config Root/http-config.tls.json

# Verify against the test certificate (OpenSSL treats the self-signed cert as its own anchor;
# `openssl verify -CAfile .test-identity/cert.pem .test-identity/cert.pem` prints OK)
/opt/homebrew/opt/curl/bin/curl --cacert .test-identity/cert.pem https://localhost:8443/
# Or skip verification entirely (any curl)
curl -k https://127.0.0.1:8443/                       # HTTP/2 via ALPN
curl -k --http1.1 -sv https://127.0.0.1:8443/ 2>&1 | grep -i 'alpn\|SSL connection'
/opt/homebrew/opt/curl/bin/curl -k --http3-only https://127.0.0.1:8443/

# Look at the handshake: ALPN, version, certificate
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername localhost -alpn h2,http/1.1 </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -E 'ALPN|Protocol|subject='
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -tls1_2 -alpn http/1.1 </dev/null    # force TLS 1.2
```

`--cacert` needs the name to match a SAN: use `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`, not the Mac's
hostname. The system `/usr/bin/curl` is built on SecureTransport; if it rejects `--cacert`,
use Homebrew curl or `-k`. Run servers you start for tests through `scripts/guarded.sh -t SECS
-- …` so they are killed on time, and stop them afterwards.

**Do not add the test certificate to a keychain or mark it trusted.** `security
add-trusted-cert`, Keychain Access, or double-clicking the certificate changes trust settings,
which raises an authorization prompt and leaves a trusted self-signed root on the machine
(its private key sits unencrypted in `.test-identity/key.pem`). Tests never need it: Swift
clients pin `cert.der`, curl uses `--cacert` or `-k`. Trusting a local CA for browser checks
is a deliberate manual step for the owner, tracked in #0072.

Other macOS prompts to keep out of the way:

| Prompt | Cause | Avoid it |
|---|---|---|
| Keychain "wants to use your confidential information" / a hung handshake | `SecPKCS12Import` without `kSecImportToMemoryOnly`, keychain lookups | Load identities only with `TLSIdentity` |
| Certificate trust settings | Trusting a certificate | Pin, `--cacert` or `-k` |
| "Accept incoming network connections?" | A fresh unsigned binary listening on a non-loopback address | Bind `127.0.0.1` / `::1` for testing ([firewall](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#binding-to-all-interfaces-and-the-firewall-prompt)) |
| Local Network | Connecting to LAN addresses | Test over loopback |

## Using TLS from a custom server

A server package (see [Choosing components](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md#a-custom-server-package))
with cleartext HTTP/1.1 and HTTPS with HTTP/2, in the style of
[`Examples/custom-server`](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Examples/custom-server/Sources/MySite/MySite.swift):

```swift
import Foundation   // ProcessInfo
import HTTP1
import HTTP2
import HTTPCore
import HTTPServer
import NetworkTransport
import StaticFiles

@main
struct SecureSite {
    static func main() async throws {
        guard let password = ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["SWS_P12_PASSWORD"] else {
            fatalError("set SWS_P12_PASSWORD")
        }
        // In memory only: SecPKCS12Import with kSecImportToMemoryOnly. Throws TLSIdentityError.
        let identity = try TLSIdentity(pkcs12Path: "certs/site.p12", password: password)
        let files = try StaticFiles(root: "Public")

        let listeners: [ServerListener] = [
            .byteStream(try BSDSocketListener(configuration: .init(host: "127.0.0.1", port: 8080)), name: "http"),
            .byteStream(name: "https") { bind in
                // bind.alpnTokens is ["h2", "http/1.1"] for the protocols below.
                try TCPListener(configuration: .init(host: "127.0.0.1", port: 8443),
                                tls: TLSConfiguration(identity: identity, minimumVersion: .v1_2,
                                                      alpn: bind.alpnTokens))
            },
        ]
        // HTTP/2 when TLS negotiates h2; HTTP/1.1 for http/1.1, no ALPN, and cleartext.
        let server = Server(listeners: listeners, protocols: [TLSNegotiated(HTTP2(), fallback: HTTP1())]) {
            HSTS()        // the middleware above
            files
        }
        try await withThrowingDiscardingTaskGroup { group in
            group.addTask { try await server.run() }
            group.addTask {
                for address in try await server.waitUntilRunning() { print("listening \(address)") }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

`ProcessInfo` needs `import Foundation` (startup only, not the request path). Add SIGINT and
SIGTERM handling as in the example (`server.requestShutdown()`). For HTTP/3 add a
`.multiplexed(name: "h3", protocol: HTTP3())` listener with the same identity and the `AltSvc`
middleware: see [HTTPS, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 in Swift](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md#https-http2-and-http3-in-swift)
and [HTTP/3 in a custom server](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/http3.md#in-a-custom-server). Use `0.0.0.0` only when the
server must be reachable from other machines.

## Troubleshooting

### Startup errors

The executable loads the identity before binding and exits with status 1 on failure. Messages
come from `TLSIdentityError`'s description and the config parser:

| Message | Meaning | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `cannot load TLS identity PATH: the file PATH cannot be read; …` | `fileUnreadable`: missing file or no permission | Check the path (relative to the config file) and its mode |
| `cannot load TLS identity PATH: wrong password (OSStatus -25293); …` | `importFailed(-25293)` (or `-25264`, MAC check failed) | Fix `password` / the `passwordEnv` variable's value |
| `cannot load TLS identity PATH: not a PKCS#12 file Security.framework can read (OSStatus N); …` | `SecPKCS12Import` rejected the file: not PKCS#12 (a PEM file, say) or an encryption it does not accept | Re-export with `-keypbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -certpbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -macalg sha1` |
| `cannot load TLS identity PATH: PKCS#12 import failed (OSStatus N); …` | Another `SecPKCS12Import` failure | Re-export the file as above |
| `cannot load TLS identity PATH: the file holds no certificate with its private key; …` | `noIdentity`: the bundle has certificates but no private key | Export with `-inkey` |
| `cannot load TLS identity PATH: the certificate's key type (…) is not supported; …` | `unsupportedKeyType`: not RSA or EC (Ed25519, DSA) | Issue an RSA or EC P-256/P-384 certificate |
| `cannot load TLS identity PATH: Network.framework cannot use the certificate and key as a TLS identity; …` | `notUsableForTLS`: `sec_identity_create` failed | Check that the key belongs to the certificate |
| `"tls.passwordEnv": environment variable NAME is not set` | The variable is missing from the server's environment | Set it (under launchd: `EnvironmentVariables`) |
| `config file …: "tls.identity" must be set to a PKCS#12 file` | `tls` without `identity` | Add it |
| `config file …: "tls.password" or "tls.passwordEnv" must be set` / `must have "password" or "passwordEnv", not both` | Password keys missing or doubled | Use exactly one |
| `"tls.port" 8080 is the cleartext port too; both are TCP` | Same TCP port twice | Pick another `tls.port` (`http3.port` may equal it: UDP) |
| `"http3" needs "tls": HTTP/3 uses the TLS identity` | `http3` without `tls` | Add `tls` |
| `cannot serve on HOST:PORTS: …` | Binding failed (port in use, `EACCES` below 1024 on a specific address) | See [ports 80 and 443](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#ports-80-and-443-without-root) |

### Handshake failures

The server logs each failed handshake at info level (`handshake with ADDRESS failed: …;
closing`, or `TLS handshake with ADDRESS timed out; closing`). Watch them with:

```bash
log stream --level info --predicate 'subsystem == "PhotonHTTP" AND category == "TLS"'
```

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| curl: `SSL certificate problem: self signed certificate` / browser warning | Expected for the test identity: use `--cacert`, `-k`, or pin |
| curl: `no alternative certificate subject name matches` | The name is not a SAN of the certificate (for the test identity: only `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`) |
| Client: `no application protocol` alert | It offered only ALPN tokens the server does not have, e.g. `h2` alone with `"http2": false` |
| `wrong version number` / garbage | A cleartext client on the TLS port, or `https://` against the cleartext port |
| Client reports `protocol version` alert | It cannot do TLS 1.2 or later (or your custom server set `minimumVersion: .v1_3`) |
| Handshake hangs, then the server resets it after 10 s | The client stalls; or, in your own code, a keychain prompt from importing without `kSecImportToMemoryOnly` (stop: see [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/AGENTS.md)) |
| Browser connects but uses `http/1.1` | HTTP/2 off, or a proxy in between does not offer `h2` |
| Browser never uses h3 | No `Alt-Svc` on HTTPS responses (HTTP/3 off), UDP port blocked, or the certificate is not trusted by the browser (#0105) |

### ALPN mismatches

`openssl s_client … -alpn h2,http/1.1` should print `ALPN protocol: h2` with HTTP/2 on, and
`No ALPN negotiated` when the client offered none (the server then runs HTTP/1.1). If a custom
server answers h2 clients with HTTP/1.1 bytes or closes them, check that the TLS listener is
built with `bind.alpnTokens` (a hand-written list can offer `h2` while no HTTP/2 protocol is
registered, or the reverse) and that `HTTP2` is registered inside `TLSNegotiated` or before
`HTTP1`.

## Standards

- [RFC 8446](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446): TLS 1.3 (and the version numbers in
  `TLSVersion`)
- [RFC 5246](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246): TLS 1.2
- [RFC 7301](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7301): TLS ALPN (`http/1.1`, `h2`; §3.2 the
  `no_application_protocol` alert)
- [RFC 9113 §3.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113#section-3.3): starting HTTP/2 for
  `https` URIs via ALPN `h2`
- [RFC 9001](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001): Using TLS to secure QUIC
- [RFC 9114 §3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114#section-3.1) and
  [RFC 7838](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7838): HTTP/3 discovery with `Alt-Svc`
- [RFC 6797](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797): HTTP Strict Transport Security
- [RFC 7292](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7292): PKCS#12


---

<!-- Source: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/http1.md (HTML: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/http1.html) -->

# HTTP/1.1

How the `HTTP1` target serves HTTP/1.1: when a connection uses it, what happens to the bytes
on a connection, which limits and timeouts apply, which status codes malformed requests get,
and how to configure it from Swift or `http-config.json`. For the server as a whole, start with
the [overview](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/overview.md).

## Where it sits

```
listener ─▶ transport ─▶ protocol registry ─▶ HTTP1.run ─▶ handler chain ─▶ response
 (BSD / NW TCP / TLS)     (ALPN or sniff)      (one per connection)  (middleware…, handler)
```

A listener accepts a connection and wraps it in a `ByteStreamTransport` (BSD sockets + kqueue
or Network.framework TCP for cleartext, Network.framework for TLS). The `Server`'s protocol
registry picks a protocol for it once. If that is HTTP/1.1, `HTTP1.run` owns the connection
until it closes: it parses each request head, calls the handler chain (the same chain HTTP/2
and HTTP/3 call), and writes the response. Middleware never sees HTTP/1.1 framing; it sees an
`HTTPRequest` and returns an `HTTPResponse`.

The target holds these pieces, each tested alone over in-memory transports:

| Type | File | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `HTTP1` | [HTTP1.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1.swift) | The `ConnectionProtocol` you register, and the per-connection loop |
| `HTTP1Configuration` | [HTTP1.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1.swift) | Buffer sizes, body limits, parser and chunked limits, timeouts |
| `HTTP1Parser`, `HTTP1ParserLimits`, `HTTP1ParseError` | [HTTP1Parser.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1Parser.swift), [HTTP1RequestHead.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1RequestHead.swift) | Incremental request-head parser and its limits and errors |
| `HTTP1Connection` | [HTTP1Connection.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1Connection.swift) | The connection state machine: keep-alive, body and error decisions. A value type with no I/O |
| `ChunkedDecoder`, `HTTP1ChunkedEncoder` | [ChunkedDecoder.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/ChunkedDecoder.swift), [HTTP1Serializer.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1Serializer.swift) | Chunked transfer coding in and out |
| `HTTP1RequestBodyReader` | [HTTP1RequestBodyReader.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1RequestBodyReader.swift) | Reads request bodies on demand while the handler runs |
| `HTTP1Serializer`, `HTTP1ResponseBodyWriter` | [HTTP1Serializer.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1Serializer.swift), [HTTP1ResponseBodyWriter.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1ResponseBodyWriter.swift) | Response heads and framing; `.stream` bodies under backpressure |
| `HTTP1Timeouts` | [HTTP1Timeouts.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1Timeouts.swift) | Header, idle, body, send and linger limits |

`HTTP1` depends only on `HTTPCore`. `HTTPServer` depends on it, so every server includes it.

## When a connection speaks HTTP/1.1

The registry picks a protocol once per connection
([ProtocolRegistry.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTPServer/ProtocolRegistry.swift)):

| Connection | Registered protocols | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Cleartext | `[HTTP1()]` or `[TLSNegotiated(HTTP2(), fallback: HTTP1())]` | HTTP/1.1, with nothing read ahead |
| Cleartext | `[HTTP2(), HTTP1()]` (h2c on) | The first bytes are sniffed: the HTTP/2 preface goes to HTTP/2, anything that starts like a request line (optional empty lines, then a method token and a space) to HTTP/1.1. The sniffed bytes are replayed to the chosen protocol |
| TLS, ALPN `http/1.1` | any | HTTP/1.1 |
| TLS, ALPN `h2` | `TLSNegotiated(HTTP2(), fallback: HTTP1())` or `[HTTP2(), HTTP1()]` | HTTP/2 |
| TLS, no ALPN, or a token no protocol lists | any | The protocol that lists `http/1.1`, the TLS default |

`TLSNegotiated(HTTP2(), fallback: HTTP1())` is one protocol that offers `h2` and `http/1.1` by
ALPN and runs HTTP/2 only when TLS negotiated `h2`; every other connection runs the fallback.
With a single protocol registered, cleartext connections are neither sniffed nor wrapped in a
replay transport, so the cleartext path costs what `HTTP1` alone costs. The shipped executable
registers exactly this unless `"http2": {"cleartext": true}`; with `"http2": false` it
registers `[HTTP1]` ([ServerProtocols.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/Photon/ServerProtocols.swift)).
[Choosing components](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md#https-http2-and-http3-in-swift) shows the Swift
side.

When sniffing is on, a client that does not send enough bytes to decide within
`ServerConfiguration.sniffTimeout` (10 s by default) is closed. Sniffing reads at most 64 bytes.

## A connection's lifecycle

One connection is one call to `HTTP1.run`. It owns the receive buffer, the parser, the
serializer, the output buffer and the state machine as locals: no actor, no task per request,
no lock. Two sibling tasks supervise it for its lifetime: a timer and a waiter on the server's
shutdown signal.

```
          ┌──────── needMoreBytes ───────┐
          ▼                              │
  idle ──bytes──▶ readingHead ──head──▶ handling ──response──▶ writing ──sent──▶ idle
    │                 │                    │                      │
    │            parse error          handler throws          close / tunnel
    ▼                 ▼                    ▼                      ▼
  closing ◀───────────┴────────────────────┘            closing / tunnelled
```

### Parsing the head

The parser scans bytes once, wherever the head is split across receives, and allocates nothing
once its field index has grown. It follows RFC 9112 strictly:

- Empty lines (CRLF) before the request line are skipped.
- Every line ends in CRLF. A bare LF or a CR without LF is an error.
- Method: 1 to 24 token characters, case-sensitive (`get` is an extension method, not `GET`).
  Extension methods such as `PROPFIND` are passed to the handler.
- Request target: bytes 0x21–0x7E, in one of the four forms of RFC 9112 §3.2. Origin form
  (`/path?query`) is the usual one. Absolute form (`http://host/path`) is accepted, without
  userinfo (`@`). Authority form (`host:port`) is accepted only for `CONNECT`, which requires
  it. Asterisk form (`*`) is accepted only for `OPTIONS`.
- Version: `HTTP/1.1` or `HTTP/1.0`.
- Field names are tokens. Whitespace before the `:` and obsolete line folding (a line starting
  with SP or HTAB) are errors. Values may contain visible characters, obs-text, SP and HTAB;
  leading and trailing whitespace is trimmed.
- After the head: HTTP/1.1 needs exactly one `Host`, and HTTP/1.0 at most one. Then the body
  framing is decided (see [Request smuggling defences](#request-smuggling-defences)).

The request the handler gets borrows the connection's receive buffer: no copy of the path,
query or fields. It is valid only while `handle` runs; `request.snapshot()` copies it.

### Keep-alive and pipelining

| Request | Connection after the response |
|---|---|
| HTTP/1.1 | Stays open unless the request's `Connection` lists `close` |
| HTTP/1.0 | Stays open only if `Connection` lists `keep-alive` |

Every response says `connection: keep-alive` or `connection: close`. The serializer writes that
field itself from the state machine's decision; a `Connection` field set by the handler is not
written as is (except on `1xx` and `.tunnel` responses, so `101` keeps the handler's
`connection: upgrade`). A handler that wants the connection closed after its response (after
an auth failure, under overload, to rebalance clients) sets `connection: close`: when that
field lists `close` (any case, any position in the list), the response says `connection: close`
and the connection closes after it, as RFC 9112 §9.6 describes; pipelined requests already read
are not answered. Any other `Connection` value is ignored: a handler cannot keep open a
connection the client or the server decided to close. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 drop the field, which
is connection-specific there, and change nothing else.

There is no limit on the number of requests per connection; the idle timeout and
`maxConnections` bound what idle clients can hold.

Pipelining is supported. Per batch the loop does one `receive`, parses every complete head the
buffer holds, calls the handler for each in order, serializes the responses into one output
buffer, and sends it with one `send`. The output is sent early once it holds 64 KiB
(`flushThreshold`), so a long pipeline of large responses does not grow it without bound.
Before a request that has a body, earlier responses are sent first. After each batch consumed
bytes are discarded, so the receive buffer does not grow across requests.

### Request bodies

The handler reads the body through `request.body`, an `AsyncSequence` of `ByteBuffer` chunks.
Bytes are received only when the handler asks for them, so a handler that reads slowly applies
TCP backpressure to the client, and memory stays at about one receive (16 KiB by default)
whatever the body size.

```swift
for try await chunk in request.body { /* … */ }        // streamed
let whole = try await request.body.collect(upTo: 1 << 20)   // or collected, with a cap
let length = request.body.knownLength                   // Content-Length, nil for chunked
let trailers = request.body.trailers                    // chunked trailers, after the last chunk
```

| Framing | How it is read |
|---|---|
| No `Content-Length`, no `Transfer-Encoding` | No body |
| `Content-Length: N` | Exactly N bytes; reads never go past the body into the next request. Above `maxBodySize`: `413` and close before the handler runs |
| `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` | Decoded chunk by chunk. Chunk extensions are checked and ignored. Trailers are checked and exposed as `request.body.trailers`. Over `maxBodySize` decoded bytes: the read throws, the response is `413` and the connection closes |

A body is readable only while the handler runs; a body kept after it returns throws
`HTTPRequestBodyError.expired`. If the handler lets a body error propagate, the connection
answers for it: `413` for too large (including `collect(upTo:)`'s own cap), `400` for a
malformed or truncated body. Either way the connection closes. A handler that catches the
error and returns its own response gets that response sent with `connection: close`.

When the handler returns without reading the whole body, the rest is read and discarded so
the next request starts at the right byte, up to 64 KiB (`maxDrainSize`). A longer rest, or a
body that failed, makes the response say `connection: close` instead.

### `Expect: 100-continue`

`HTTP/1.1 100 Continue` is sent when the handler first reads a body that has not arrived yet. A
handler that rejects the request without reading (a `401`, say) sends no `100`; since the
client was never asked to send the body, the response says `close`. If body bytes already
arrived with the head, no `100` is sent. An expectation other than `100-continue` gets
`417 Expectation Failed` and close. HTTP/1.0 requests cannot receive `100`, so their
`100-continue` is ignored.

### Responses and framing

The serializer writes the status line, the handler's fields in order (names in lowercase), a
`date` field unless the response has one, the framing, and `connection`. It owns framing: a
handler's `transfer-encoding` and `connection` fields are not written, nor is its
`content-length` where the serializer writes its own.

| Response body | Framing |
|---|---|
| `.empty` | `content-length: 0` |
| `.bytes(b)` | `content-length` and the bytes, in the same send as the head |
| `.file(region)` | `content-length`; the head is sent, then the file with `sendFile` (`sendfile(2)` on the BSD transport) in slices of at most 1 MiB |
| `.stream(length: n, writer:)` | `content-length: n`; each `write` is one send. Writing more or fewer than `n` bytes aborts the connection |
| `.stream(length: nil, writer:)` | `transfer-encoding: chunked`, one chunk per `write`, then the last chunk. To an HTTP/1.0 request: no framing field and `connection: close`, and the body ends when the connection closes |
| `.tunnel` | No framing field and no `connection` field; see [Upgrades and tunnels](#upgrades-and-tunnels) |

Each `.stream` write returns only once the transport accepted the bytes, so a writer faster
than the client slows down instead of buffering. A writer that throws after the head was sent
aborts the connection (the client sees a truncated body, not a second response).

### HEAD, 204 and 304

| Response | What is sent |
|---|---|
| To `HEAD` | The headers a `GET` would get, with the `content-length` of the content when it is known (`.bytes`, `.file`, `.stream` with a length), and no body. A `.stream` writer or file is never run |
| `304 Not Modified` | Same as `HEAD`: headers only |
| `204 No Content` | No `content-length`, no body |
| `1xx` | The handler's fields only: no `date`, framing or `connection` |

For an `.empty` or chunked body to `HEAD` or `304`, the handler's own `content-length` passes
through, so it can state the length a `GET` would have had.

### When the connection closes

| Cause | What the client gets |
|---|---|
| Request asked for `close`, or HTTP/1.0 without `keep-alive` | The response with `connection: close`, then close |
| Handler's response lists `close` in its `Connection` field | That response with `connection: close`, then close; pipelined requests already read are not answered |
| Malformed head | The error status (below) with an empty body and `connection: close` |
| Handler throws, or returns a field that fails validation (see [Request smuggling defences](#request-smuggling-defences)) | `500` with `connection: close`. Responses already serialized for earlier pipelined requests go out first |
| Client closes between requests or mid-head | Nothing; quiet close |
| Receive or send fails | Nothing; the connection ends |
| Server draining | See [Running on a Mac](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#shutdown-restart-and-reload). A connection between requests (idle, or mid-head) closes at once. A request in flight finishes and its response says `close`; pipelined requests not yet started get no response |

**Lingering close.** When the connection closes with request bytes possibly unread (an error
response, an unread body, dropped pipelined requests, a `408`), the server half-closes its
output and reads and discards input for up to `timeouts.linger` (2 s) or 1 MiB
(`maxLingerSize`). Without this, the client's unread bytes would make the kernel reset the
connection, and the client could lose the error response.

Error responses for malformed heads, `413` for a `Content-Length` over the limit, `417`, the
timeout `408`, and the `500` (or `413`/`400` for a failed body) for a handler that throws are
written by `HTTP1` itself, without calling the handler chain. They still go through the chain's
`ProtocolResponseObserver`s (#0139), which the server finds at startup like connection
observers:

- `ErrorPages` gives every one of them its page, by its usual rules (no page for `HEAD`; the
  page of a `GET` when the head could not be parsed).
- `AccessLog` logs every one with the status and body bytes sent. When the request line is
  unknown (an unparsable head, a header timeout) the line has `-` in its place, as Apache logs
  a bad request: `192.0.2.7 - - [13/Nov/2026:10:00:00 +0000] "-" 400 -`. A handler that throws
  is logged once, by the runner, with the status actually sent.

A response replaced with `500` because a field would split it (#0136) is the exception: the
access log keeps the line it wrote when the handler returned (with the handler's status), and
the replacement is reported in the `os` log.

## Limits and timeouts

| Limit | Default | Swift | `http-config.json` | When exceeded |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Request line | 8 KiB (excluding CRLF) | `HTTP1ParserLimits.maxRequestLineLength` | – | `414` + close |
| Head size (request line through final CRLF) | 16 KiB | `HTTP1ParserLimits.maxHeadBytes` | – | `431` + close |
| Header fields per head | 100 | `HTTP1ParserLimits.maxHeaderCount` | – | `431` + close |
| Method length | 24 bytes | fixed (`HTTPMethod.Token.maximumLength`) | – | `501` + close |
| Request body | 10 MiB | `HTTP1Configuration.maxBodySize` | `maxBodySize` (alias `maxRequestSize`) | `413` + close |
| Unread body drained before the next request | 64 KiB | `HTTP1Configuration.maxDrainSize` | – | Response says `close` |
| Chunk size | 1 TiB | `ChunkedDecoderLimits.maxChunkSize` | – | `400` + close (`maxBodySize` applies first in practice) |
| Chunk extensions per chunk | 1 KiB | `ChunkedDecoderLimits.maxExtensionLength` | – | `400` + close |
| Trailer section | 8 KiB, 32 fields | `ChunkedDecoderLimits.maxTrailerBytes`, `.maxTrailerFields` | – | `400` + close |
| Bytes per receive | 16 KiB | `HTTP1Configuration.receiveSize` | – | – |
| Output sent early during a pipelined batch | 64 KiB | `HTTP1Configuration.flushThreshold` | – | – |
| Bytes discarded while lingering | 1 MiB | `HTTP1Configuration.maxLingerSize` | – | Close |
| Header timeout: a head must complete this long after its first byte | 10 s | `HTTP1Timeouts.header` | `timeouts.header` | `408` + close |
| Idle timeout: no byte of the next head (also before the first request) | 5 s | `HTTP1Timeouts.idle` | `timeouts.idle` (legacy `keepAliveTimeout`) | Silent close |
| Body timeout: wait for request body bytes, restarted on progress | 30 s | `HTTP1Timeouts.body` | `timeouts.body` | `408` + close |
| Send timeout: one send waiting for the client to accept bytes, restarted per send | 30 s | `HTTP1Timeouts.send` | `timeouts.send` | Connection reset (abort) |
| Linger after an error response | 2 s | `HTTP1Timeouts.linger` | `timeouts.linger` | Close |
| Connections at once (all protocols) | 1024 | `ServerConfiguration.maxConnections` | `maxConnections` | New connections wait in the listen backlog |

Notes:

- The header timeout is not renewed by progress, so a client that trickles a head one byte at
  a time (slowloris) is closed when it passes. Handler time is never limited.
- `nil` in Swift, and `0` or `null` in the config file, turns a timeout off.
  `HTTP1Timeouts.disabled` turns them all off.
- Large `.bytes` and `.file` bodies are sent in slices of 1 MiB, each under its own send
  timeout, so the send limit catches a stalled client, not a slow download.
- The idle timeout also closes idle HTTP/2 connections in the executable (with `GOAWAY`).
- The parser, drain, chunked and buffer limits are not in `http-config.json`; set them in Swift.

## Errors

A malformed head gets one of these statuses, with an empty body and `connection: close`
([HTTP1RequestHead.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP1/HTTP1RequestHead.swift), `HTTP1ParseError`):

| Status | Cause |
|---|---|
| `400 Bad Request` | Invalid method token; invalid request target (bad byte, wrong form for the method, userinfo in absolute form, `CONNECT` without `host:port`); malformed version; bare LF or CR; invalid field name; whitespace before `:`; obsolete line folding; invalid byte in a field value (NUL, DEL, other controls); no `Host` on HTTP/1.1; more than one `Host`; both `Transfer-Encoding` and `Content-Length`; `Transfer-Encoding` whose last coding is not `chunked`, that repeats `chunked`, or on HTTP/1.0; invalid `Content-Length`; `Content-Length` values that differ |
| `414 URI Too Long` | Request line over `maxRequestLineLength` |
| `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` | Head over `maxHeadBytes`, or more than `maxHeaderCount` fields |
| `501 Not Implemented` | Method longer than 24 bytes; a transfer coding other than `chunked` before the final `chunked` (`gzip, chunked`) |
| `505 HTTP Version Not Supported` | A well-formed `HTTP/d.d` other than 1.0 and 1.1 |

After a valid head:

| Status | Cause |
|---|---|
| `413 Content Too Large` | `Content-Length` over `maxBodySize` (before the handler runs); a chunked body that grows past it; a handler's `collect(upTo:)` cap exceeded |
| `400 Bad Request` | A malformed chunked body (bad chunk size, missing CRLF, invalid extension or trailer), or a body cut short by the client |
| `408 Request Timeout` | Header or body timeout |
| `417 Expectation Failed` | `Expect` with anything other than `100-continue` |
| `500 Internal Server Error` | The handler threw, or returned a `.tunnel` body with a `1xx` status other than `101` |

### Request smuggling defences

Request smuggling relies on two parsers disagreeing about where a body ends. The parser takes
the strict reading of RFC 9112 everywhere:

- **`Transfer-Encoding` with `Content-Length`** is rejected with `400`, not resolved in favour
  of one of them.
- **`Transfer-Encoding` must end in `chunked`**, exactly once. `chunked, chunked`, `gzip` alone
  and `chunked, gzip` are `400`; `gzip, chunked` is `501` (an unsupported coding). HTTP/1.0
  requests may not use `Transfer-Encoding` at all.
- **`Content-Length`** must be decimal digits. Several fields or list elements are accepted
  only if every value is the same (`5, 5`); different values are `400`.
- **Line endings** must be CRLF; a bare LF or CR anywhere in the head, or in a chunk-size or
  trailer line, is an error.
- **Obsolete line folding** and **whitespace before `:`** are rejected, so a field cannot hide
  inside another or be read under a different name.
- **`Host`**: exactly one on HTTP/1.1, at most one on HTTP/1.0.
- **Every error closes the connection** (with a lingering close), so bytes after a bad
  request are never parsed as the next request.
- **Body reads never cross the boundary**: a `Content-Length` body receives at most the bytes
  still owed; bytes received past the end of a chunked body go back to the receive buffer for
  the next head.

The test-support `ReferenceHTTP1Parser` implements the same rules independently, and
`HTTP1DifferentialTests` checks that both parsers agree over a corpus of valid and invalid
requests split at every byte offset
([Tests/HTTP1Tests](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/tree/main/Tests/HTTP1Tests)).

On the response side, every handler response is checked before it is written, in release
builds too (`HTTPFieldValidation`, #0136): each field name must be a token, and no field value
or custom reason phrase may hold CR, LF, NUL, another control byte or DEL (a tab is fine). A
response that fails is never written as is: it is replaced with a bare `500` with
`connection: close`, like a handler that throws, and an error is logged (`os` log, subsystem
`PhotonHTTP`, category `HTTP`). So a handler that copies decoded request bytes into a
`location` cannot split the response, but it gets a `500`; validate or encode such values to
answer properly. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 run the same check and answer the stream with a bare `500`.
Code that serializes responses itself uses `HTTP1Serializer.writeValidated`, which throws
instead of writing; chunked trailers that fail the check are dropped.

## Upgrades and tunnels

A handler takes over the connection by returning a `.tunnel` body. `HTTP1` sends the head,
then hands the byte stream to the closure, replaying any bytes the client sent after the
request. No HTTP/1.1 limit or timeout applies to a tunnel, and a server drain does not
interrupt it: the closure gets the shutdown signal in its `TunnelContext` and should end itself
when it fires; a tunnel still running at the drain deadline is cancelled.

```swift
HTTPResponse(status: .switchingProtocols, headers: upgradeHeaders, body: .tunnel { transport, context in
    // read and write `transport` until done; watch `context.shutdown`
})
```

- **WebSockets**: `WebSocketUpgrade` answers an RFC 6455 handshake on HTTP/1.1 with
  `101 Switching Protocols` and runs the session over the tunnel. See
  [WebSockets](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/websockets.md) and [Dynamic websites](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/dynamic-sites.md#websockets).
- **Proxied upgrades**: `ReverseProxy` mounts with `"websocket": true` tunnel the upgraded
  connection to the upstream. See [the proxy reference](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/dynamic-sites.md#proxy-mount-reference).
- **`CONNECT`**: the parser accepts `CONNECT host:port` and passes it to the handler chain, and
  a `2xx` response with a `.tunnel` body is sent without framing. No shipped component answers
  `CONNECT`: there is no forward proxy.
- **h2c Upgrade** (`Upgrade: h2c`) is not supported. Cleartext HTTP/2 is available only with
  prior knowledge (`"http2": {"cleartext": true}`), which is chosen by sniffing before HTTP/1.1
  runs.

## Using HTTP1 in your own server

Register `HTTP1` (or `TLSNegotiated(HTTP2(), fallback: HTTP1())` when you also serve HTTPS
with HTTP/2) with a `Server`. Pass an `HTTP1Configuration` to change limits:

```swift
import HTTP1
import HTTPCore
import HTTPServer
import NetworkTransport
import Router

let http1 = HTTP1(configuration: HTTP1Configuration(
    parserLimits: HTTP1ParserLimits(maxRequestLineLength: 4 * 1024, maxHeaderCount: 64,
                                    maxHeadBytes: 8 * 1024),
    maxBodySize: 50 * 1024 * 1024,
    timeouts: HTTP1Timeouts(header: .seconds(5), idle: .seconds(15))))   // others keep defaults

let router = try Router {
    POST("/upload") { request, _ in
        var received = 0
        for try await chunk in request.body { received += chunk.readableBytes }   // read on demand
        return HTTPResponse(status: .ok, body: .bytes(ByteBuffer(bytes: Array("\(received)\n".utf8))))
    }
    GET("/count") { _, _ in
        // No length: chunked on HTTP/1.1, close-delimited on HTTP/1.0.
        HTTPResponse(status: .ok, body: .stream(length: nil, writer: { writer in
            for i in 1...3 { try await writer.write(ByteBuffer(bytes: Array("\(i)\n".utf8))) }
        }))
    }
}
let listener = try BSDSocketListener(configuration: .init(host: "127.0.0.1", port: 8080))
let server = Server(configuration: ServerConfiguration(maxConnections: 512),
                    listeners: [listener], protocols: [http1]) {
    router
}
try await server.run()
```

This type-checks against this checkout. A complete package with signal handling, static files
and WebSockets is
[Examples/custom-server](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Examples/custom-server/Sources/MySite/MySite.swift), walked
through in [Choosing components](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md#a-custom-server-package).

If you load `http-config.json` with `ConfigFile`, `settings.http1Configuration` gives the
`HTTP1Configuration` the executable uses (`maxBodySize` and `timeouts` from the file, every
other field at its default), so you can start from it and change the rest:

```swift
var configuration = settings.http1Configuration
configuration.parserLimits.maxHeadBytes = 32 * 1024
let http1 = HTTP1(configuration: configuration)
```

## Configuring the executable

HTTP/1.1 is always on. Its keys in `http-config.json`, with their defaults:

```json
{
  "maxBodySize": 10485760,
  "timeouts": {
    "header": 10,
    "idle": 5,
    "body": 30,
    "send": 30,
    "linger": 2
  },
  "maxConnections": 1024
}
```

- Durations are seconds; fractions are allowed; `0` or `null` turns a limit off; a missing key
  keeps its default. Unknown keys under `timeouts` print a warning and are ignored.
- `maxBodySize` also sets HTTP/2's body limit unless `http2.maxRequestBodySize` is set.
- These keys need a restart: `SIGHUP` reloads the handler chain but reports changes to
  `timeouts`, `maxBodySize`, `maxConnections` and `http2` as ignored.
- The full reference, including legacy aliases, is in
  [Running on a Mac](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#listening-and-limits).

For long uploads over slow links raise `timeouts.body`; for long-polling or server-sent events
raise or turn off `timeouts.send` only if clients stall reading, since the send timeout
restarts with every send. Handler time itself is never limited.

## Performance

All numbers are from the owner's Apple M4 Pro over loopback, on a shared machine; each record
gives its load average and method.

| What | Result | Record |
|---|---|---|
| Head parse, 10-header browser request | About 130 ns, 0 allocations; minimal request about 27 ns | [M1.3-parser](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/M1.3-parser.md), [M-final-micro](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/M-final-micro.md) |
| Serialize a `200` with 5 headers | About 75 ns, 0 allocations; a chunk header about 23 ns | [M-final-micro](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/M-final-micro.md) |
| Connection loop per request (parse, handler call, serialize, send bookkeeping) | About 250 ns keep-alive, 177 ns with 16 pipelined requests per receive, 0 allocations; the timeout supervision added no measurable cost | [M3.3-timeouts](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/M3.3-timeouts.md), [M3.1-h1conn](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/M3.1-h1conn.md) |
| Request bodies | Echoing a 1 KiB `POST` body costs a few percent against a `GET`; a 4 MiB body keeps memory at one receive | [M3.2-bodies](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/M3.2-bodies.md) |
| Static files over keep-alive | About 93k req/s at 16 connections, 97k at 64 | [compare-servers-final](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/compare-servers-final.md) |
| New connections | About 22k/s on the BSD listener | [M3-accept](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/M3-accept.md) |

The [performance notes](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/performance.md) summarize the rest. What matters for HTTP/1.1:

- Keep-alive is where the server is fast; closing after every response is dominated by TCP
  setup. Leave the idle timeout long enough for your clients to reuse connections.
- Keep the default `TLSNegotiated` registration (`http2.cleartext` off) so cleartext
  connections are not sniffed.
- Prefer `.file` for files (`sendfile(2)` on the BSD transport) and `.bytes` for small
  in-memory bodies (sent with the head in one send); `.stream` costs one send per write.

## Standards

- [RFC 9110](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110): HTTP Semantics (methods, status codes,
  `Expect`, `HEAD`, `204`/`304` rules, `Content-Length`)
- [RFC 9112](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112): HTTP/1.1 (message syntax, request-target
  forms, body framing and chunked coding, persistence, pipelining, lingering close)
- [RFC 7301](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7301): TLS ALPN (`http/1.1`, `h2`)
- [RFC 6455](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455): The WebSocket Protocol (the HTTP/1.1
  upgrade)


---

<!-- Source: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/http3.md (HTML: https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/http3.html) -->

# HTTP/3

PhotonHTTP serves HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) over QUIC. It has no QUIC stack of its own: QUIC,
TLS 1.3, loss recovery and congestion control come from Network.framework (`NWProtocolQUIC`).
HTTP/3 framing, stream handling and QPACK header compression are written in Swift in the
`HTTP3` and `QPACK` targets. The QUIC listener runs next to the TCP listeners in the same
`Server`, and HTTPS responses tell clients where to find it with an `Alt-Svc` header.

Why Network.framework: implementing QUIC ourselves would need a TLS 1.3 server that exposes
its handshake secrets (no public API does), packet protection, RFC 9002 recovery, migration
and anti-amplification. ROADMAP §6 chose Option A (Network.framework) after a spike;
Option B (our own QUIC) was rejected. The spike's findings are in
[quic-spike.md](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/spikes/quic-spike.md), and the adapter's in
[notes/nw-transport.md](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/notes/nw-transport.md).

## How it fits together

| Layer | Where | Role |
|---|---|---|
| QUIC listener | `QUICListener` ([NetworkTransport](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/NetworkTransport/QUICListener.swift)) | `NWListener` with `newConnectionGroupHandler`: one `NWConnectionGroup`, so one `QUICConnection`, per QUIC connection. Binds UDP with `requiredLocalEndpoint` |
| QUIC connection | `QUICConnection`, `QUICStreamTransport` | A `MultiplexedTransport`: inbound streams as a demand-driven sequence, our own unidirectional streams, FIN, RESET_STREAM / STOP_SENDING codes, MAX_STREAMS credit |
| QUIC options | `QUICConfiguration` ([source](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/NetworkTransport/QUICConfiguration.swift)) | ALPN (`h3`), flow-control windows, stream limits, idle timeout |
| HTTP/3 | `HTTP3`, `H3Configuration` ([Sources/HTTP3](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP3/HTTP3.swift)) | Control and QPACK streams, SETTINGS, request streams to `HTTPHandler`, GOAWAY, limits |
| QPACK | `QPACKEncoder`, `QPACKDecoder`, `QPACKDynamicDecoder` ([Sources/QPACK](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/tree/main/Sources/QPACK)) | Static table, Huffman, the decoder side of the dynamic table |
| Discovery | `AltSvc` middleware ([AltSvc.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP3/AltSvc.swift)) | `Alt-Svc: h3=":PORT"; ma=SECONDS` on HTTPS responses |

`HTTP3` is a `MultiplexedConnectionProtocol`; a `ServerListener.multiplexed(...)` entry
pairs it with the QUIC listener. The handler chain is the same one HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 use,
so every component works over HTTP/3 unchanged. Requests report `version` `.http3` and
the connection's negotiated ALPN is `h3`.

## Requirements

- **A TLS identity.** QUIC always uses TLS 1.3, so HTTP/3 needs the same PKCS#12 identity as
  HTTPS, loaded in memory only. In `http-config.json`, `http3` without `tls` fails at startup
  (`"http3" needs "tls"`). See the TLS guide, [tls.md](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/tls.md), and
  [HTTPS with a PKCS#12 identity](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#https-with-a-pkcs12-identity).
- **A UDP port.** By default the TLS port number, over UDP (TCP and UDP ports do not clash;
  the spike confirmed both listen on one number). Any firewall or router in front of the Mac
  must pass UDP as well as TCP.
- **macOS 15 or later**, like the rest of the package. The executable must be built with the
  `HTTP3` package trait, which is on by default; without it an `http3` key fails at startup
  ("this build has no HTTP/3"). See [package traits](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md#package-traits-for-the-executable).

Binding rules are the same as for TCP: `QUICListener` defaults to `127.0.0.1`, and loopback
never triggers the macOS firewall prompt. Binding `0.0.0.0` or `::` with an unsigned, freshly
built binary can ([the firewall prompt](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#binding-to-all-interfaces-and-the-firewall-prompt)).
Tests and local checks therefore bind loopback and port 0.

## Turning it on in `http-config.json`

```json
{
  "host": "127.0.0.1",
  "port": 8080,
  "root": "Public",
  "tls": { "identity": "certs/server.p12", "passwordEnv": "SWS_P12_PASSWORD", "port": 8443 },
  "http3": true
}
```

`"http3": true` uses every default. The object form:

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `http3.enabled` | bool | `true` | `false` turns it off (as do `"http3": false` and `null`) |
| `http3.port` | integer 0–65535 or `null` | TLS port number | UDP port. `null` or absent takes the TLS listener's bound port, including one picked when `tls.port` is 0 |
| `http3.altSvcMaxAge` | integer seconds | `86400` | `ma` of the `Alt-Svc` header |
| `http3.qpackMaxTableCapacity` | integer 0–1048576 | `0` | QPACK dynamic table offered to clients; `0` decodes with the static table only |
| `http3.qpackBlockedStreams` | integer 0–1000 | `0` | Request streams that may wait for QPACK inserts at once (only with a table) |

The full config reference is in [Running on a Mac](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/running-on-a-mac.md#tls-http2-and-http3).
`http3` is a restart-only key: `SIGHUP` reports a change to it and ignores it.

What else the executable sets (`makeListeners` in
[ServerMain.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/Photon/ServerMain.swift)):

- Listeners bind in order cleartext, TLS, QUIC, and print `listening HOST:PORT (h3)`.
- The QUIC listener offers ALPN `h3` and uses the default `QUICConfiguration`.
- `AltSvc` is the outermost element of the chain (the [chain table](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/overview.md#the-chain-the-executable-builds)),
  added only when `http3` is on, and rendered once the UDP port is bound.
- `H3Configuration` keeps its defaults (tables below) except the two QPACK keys and
  `timeouts.closeLinger`, which is set to `drainTimeout` (at least 1 s; 30 s when
  `drainTimeout` is `null`).
- The general `maxBodySize` and `timeouts` keys are **not** applied to HTTP/3. HTTP/3 keeps
  its own 10 MiB body limit and its own timeouts, whatever those keys say.
- `maxConnections` is shared by every listener, so QUIC connections count against it too.

## How clients find it: Alt-Svc

Browsers do not try QUIC first. They connect over TCP and TLS, see

```
alt-svc: h3=":8443"; ma=86400
```

on the response, and use HTTP/3 for that origin for the next `ma` seconds (RFC 7838,
RFC 9114 §3.1.1). The `AltSvc` middleware adds the header only to responses on TLS
connections that are not HTTP/3: HTTPS over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2. Cleartext responses never
carry it (a client must not take an alternative for an `https` origin from an
unauthenticated connection), and HTTP/3 responses do not repeat it. It is added to every
such response, error pages included, at the cost of one atomic load and a copy of the
pre-rendered bytes.

```swift
let altSvc = AltSvc(port: 8443, maxAge: 86_400)  // port known up front
let altSvc = AltSvc(maxAge: 86_400)              // or: nothing until advertise(port:)
altSvc.advertise(port: boundPort)                 // the first call wins
```

## Streams

### Connection setup and SETTINGS

For each connection the server opens three unidirectional streams: its control stream
(type `0x00`, starting with SETTINGS), and its QPACK encoder (`0x02`) and decoder (`0x03`)
streams. They stay open for the life of the connection. The SETTINGS it sends:

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| `SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY` | `qpackMaxTableCapacity` (default 0) |
| `SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE` | `maxFieldSectionSize` (default 16,384) |
| `SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS` | `qpackBlockedStreams` when the table is on, else 0 |
| `SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL` | `1`, only when extended CONNECT is enabled (below); otherwise not sent |

From the client, the server accepts exactly one control stream (SETTINGS first, once), one
QPACK encoder and one decoder stream. A second one of any of them, or a client push stream,
is `H3_STREAM_CREATION_ERROR`; a missing first SETTINGS is `H3_MISSING_SETTINGS`; one of them
closing is `H3_CLOSED_CRITICAL_STREAM`. HTTP/2-only frame types and setting identifiers are
errors as RFC 9114 requires. Reserved (GREASE) and unknown unidirectional streams are refused
with STOP_SENDING `H3_STREAM_CREATION_ERROR`; unknown frames are skipped without buffering.
The peer's `SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE` is honoured: a response head larger than it is
replaced by a bare `500`.

The server never pushes. It tracks the client's `MAX_PUSH_ID` only to validate
`CANCEL_PUSH`.

### Request streams

Each client-initiated bidirectional stream is one request: HEADERS, optional DATA, optional
trailers. The handler runs as a child task of the stream's task, next to a body reader that
feeds `request.body` under backpressure (the reader stops reading the QUIC stream while
`bodyQueueCapacity` chunks wait). Request trailers reach `HTTPRequestBody.trailers`.
`priority` request fields and `PRIORITY_UPDATE` frames (RFC 9218) are applied (see
[Known limitations](#known-limitations) for what they can change).

Every failure is signalled as the `H3Failure` table in
[H3Failure.swift](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/Sources/HTTP3/H3Failure.swift) says: a stream error resets one
stream with a code; a connection error closes QUIC with a code. Cancellation works both ways
(#0104): a client RESET_STREAM or STOP_SENDING cancels the handler's task (even while it is
still computing, since `QUICStreamTransport` watches for peer aborts), and a handler that is
cancelled or throws `CancellationError` resets its stream with `H3_REQUEST_CANCELLED`. A
response body that fails after its head was sent is reset with `H3_INTERNAL_ERROR`, so a
truncated response never looks complete.

### GOAWAY and graceful shutdown

When the server drains (`requestShutdown()`, or SIGINT/SIGTERM in the executable) or a
connection has had no open request for `timeouts.idle`:

1. The server sends GOAWAY with the next unprocessed client stream ID. With
   `timeouts.goawayGrace` set, it first sends GOAWAY with the largest possible ID
   (2^62 − 4), waits the grace period, then sends the final one (RFC 9114 §5.2).
2. Streams at or above that ID are reset with `H3_REQUEST_REJECTED` (safe to retry);
   requests below it run to completion.
3. When the last one finishes, or `timeouts.drain` passes, the server waits
   `timeouts.closeLinger` (or until the client closes) so the client can read the GOAWAY and
   the last responses, then closes with `H3_NO_ERROR`.

The server's own `drainTimeout` still bounds the whole drain: at that deadline every
connection is cancelled. See [Lifecycle](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/overview.md#lifecycle).

### Extended CONNECT and WebSockets (RFC 9220)

WebSockets run over HTTP/3 with extended CONNECT. `HTTP3` advertises
`SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL = 1` when the handler chain contains an
`ExtendedConnectProvider`, which `WebSocketUpgrade` is, and so is a `ReverseProxy` with a
`websocket` mount. `H3Configuration.enableConnectProtocol = true` forces it on. Without
it, a request carrying `:protocol` is malformed.

An extended CONNECT reaches the handler like any request, with `request.connectProtocol`
set. A `2xx` response with a `.tunnel` body keeps the request stream open as a byte stream:
DATA payloads in, one DATA frame per send out, FIN as end of stream. Request body limits do
not apply to a tunnel; the send timeout does. The same `WebSocketUpgrade` endpoint serves
HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3; see the [WebSockets guide](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/websockets.md).

## QPACK

**Responses** are encoded with the static table only (RFC 9204 Appendix A, 99 entries):
an indexed line when the table has the name and value, a name reference when it has the
name, a literal otherwise. Strings are Huffman-coded when that is shorter. `authorization`,
`cookie` and `set-cookie` are always literals with the never-indexed bit. The encoder never
inserts into a dynamic table, so the server's encoder stream carries only its type byte.

**Requests** are decoded with the static table by default. The server advertises
`SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY = 0`, any dynamic reference is
`QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED`, and nothing is shared between request streams.

**The dynamic table** (decoder side, #0106) is off by default and turned on by a non-zero
capacity:

```json
"http3": { "qpackMaxTableCapacity": 4096, "qpackBlockedStreams": 16 }
```

```swift
H3Configuration(qpackMaxTableCapacity: 4_096, qpackBlockedStreams: 16)
```

With it on, the connection keeps a table (a ring over one byte arena of twice the capacity,
sized once) behind a `Mutex`, reads the client's encoder stream (Set Dynamic Table Capacity,
Insert With Name Reference, Insert With Literal Name, Duplicate), and sends Section
Acknowledgment, Stream Cancellation and Insert Count Increment on its decoder stream. A
request whose field section refers to inserts that have not arrived yet waits for them; that
wait counts against `timeouts.header`, and at most `qpackBlockedStreams` requests may wait
(one more is `QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED`). Homebrew curl (nghttp3) uses the table when it is
offered (`H3CurlTests.curlUsesTheQPACKDynamicTable`).

It is off by default because it adds connection-shared state, a lock per field section and
blocked streams. Decoding a dynamic section serializes head decoding across the streams of
one connection.

## Limits, timeouts and abuse defences

[HTTP2.md](https://github.com/brennanMKE/PhotonHTTP/blob/main/docs/HTTP2.md#http3-default-limits-0102) ("HTTP/3 default limits" and "HTTP/3
abuse limits") is the authoritative list, with the wire code for each. In summary, for a
custom server (`H3Configuration`, `H3Timeouts`, `H3AbuseLimits`); in the executable only the
two QPACK values and `closeLinger` are configurable.

### `H3Configuration`

| Setting | Default | When it is exceeded |
|---|---|---|
| `maxConcurrentRequestStreams` | 100 | QUIC MAX_STREAMS is raised to this at the start and by one per finished request; a stream beyond it is reset `H3_REQUEST_REJECTED` |
| `maxFieldSectionSize` | 16,384 | `431` when the pseudo-header fields make a valid request, else `H3_MESSAGE_ERROR` |
| `maxEncodedFieldSectionLength` | 65,536 | One HEADERS frame (the only frame buffered whole): connection error `H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD` |
| `maxRequestBodySize` | 10 MiB | `413` (declared `content-length` before the handler runs; an undeclared body when it grows past) |
| `maxUnreadBodySize` | 64 KiB | Unread request body discarded after the response; past it, STOP_SENDING `H3_NO_ERROR` |
| `bodyQueueCapacity` | 4 chunks | Read-ahead between the stream and the handler |
| `receiveSize` | 16 KiB | Most bytes asked for per stream receive |
| `qpackMaxTableCapacity` | 0 | Dynamic table off; at most 1 MiB |
| `qpackBlockedStreams` | 0 | One more blocked stream is `QPACK_DECOMPRESSION_FAILED` |
| `enableConnectProtocol` | `false` | Turned on automatically by an `ExtendedConnectProvider` in the chain |

### `H3Timeouts`

Handler time itself is never limited. `nil` turns a limit off.

| Timeout | Default | Runs while | When it passes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `header` | 10 s | A request stream has not delivered its HEADERS (not renewed by progress) | RESET_STREAM `H3_REQUEST_REJECTED` |
| `idle` | 30 s | The connection has no open request | GOAWAY, then close `H3_NO_ERROR` |
| `body` | 30 s | The handler waits for request body bytes (renewed per chunk) | `408`, or `H3_REQUEST_CANCELLED` once the response started |
| `send` | 30 s | One response send waits (slow reader or send budget) | RESET_STREAM `H3_REQUEST_CANCELLED` |
| `unreadBody` | 2 s | Unread body is discarded after the response | STOP_SENDING `H3_NO_ERROR` |
| `drain` | off | Requests below the final GOAWAY finish | Close `H3_NO_ERROR` (off: the server's drain deadline decides) |
| `goawayGrace` | off | Between the provisional and the final GOAWAY | The final GOAWAY |
| `closeLinger` | 1 s (executable: `drainTimeout`) | After the drain, until the client closes | Close `H3_NO_ERROR` |

### `H3AbuseLimits`

Counted per connection in a fixed window (`window`, 10 s) that starts at the first event.
Each `H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD` below closes the connection. `nil` turns a limit off;
`H3AbuseLimits.disabled` turns them all off.

| Limit | Default | Counts |
|---|---|---|
| `maxAbortedRequestsPerWindow` | 100 | Rapid reset: request streams the client resets or stops before the response completes, or ends without a request |
| `maxIgnoredUniStreamsPerWindow` | 16 | Reserved and unknown unidirectional streams |
| `maxQPACKInstructionsPerWindow` | 1,000 | Instructions on the client's QPACK encoder and decoder streams |
| `maxControlFramesPerWindow` | 1,000 | Control-stream frames, unknown ones included |
| `maxUnknownRequestFramesPerWindow` | 1,000 | Reserved and unknown frames on request streams |
| `maxUnknownFrameLength` | 16 KiB | Declared length of one unknown frame, any stream (skipped, never buffered) |
| `maxConnectionSendBuffer` | 4 MiB | Response bytes in sends not yet completed, across the connection; further sends wait, and `timeouts.send` resets stalled streams |
| `maxIdleConnections` | 1,000 | Connections of one `HTTP3` value with no open request; the longest-idle one is shut down gracefully |

A QPACK decoder-stream backlog over 64 KiB (the client does not read it) is also
`H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD`.

### QUIC transport (`QUICConfiguration`, `QUICListener.Configuration`)

These bound what a client can make Network.framework buffer.

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `maxStreamsBidirectional` | 100 | `initial_max_streams_bidi`; replenished by the adapter as streams finish (Network.framework does not) |
| `maxStreamsUnidirectional` | 8 | `initial_max_streams_uni` (HTTP/3 needs at least 3) |
| `initialMaxData` | 4 MiB | Connection receive window |
| `initialMaxStreamDataBidirectionalRemote` / `Local` | 256 KiB | Per-stream receive window |
| `initialMaxStreamDataUnidirectional` | 64 KiB | Per unidirectional stream |
| `idleTimeoutMilliseconds` | 30,000 | QUIC `max_idle_timeout` |
| `sendChunkSize` | 64 KiB | A larger send is split; each chunk waits for Network.framework to accept it |
| `pendingStreamLimit` | streams + 2 | Inbound streams held before HTTP/3 takes them; more are reset `H3_REQUEST_REJECTED` |
| `pendingConnectionLimit` (listener) | 64 | Accepted connections not yet taken; more are closed at once |

## In a custom server

Add the `HTTP3` product (it brings `QPACK`) next to `HTTPServer` and `NetworkTransport` in
your package, as in [A custom server package](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md#a-custom-server-package).
This server serves HTTPS (HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 by ALPN) and HTTP/3 on the same port number,
with a tuned `H3Configuration`:

```swift
import HTTP1
import HTTP2
import HTTP3
import HTTPCore
import HTTPServer
import NetworkTransport
import StaticFiles

@main
struct MySite {
    static func main() async throws {
        // PKCS#12 loaded in memory only; never the keychain.
        let identity = try TLSIdentity(pkcs12Path: ".test-identity/server.p12", password: "sws-test-password")
        let files = try StaticFiles(root: "Public")
        let altSvc = AltSvc(maxAge: 3_600)   // adds nothing until advertise(port:)

        var h3 = H3Configuration(maxRequestBodySize: 1 << 20,
                                 qpackMaxTableCapacity: 4_096, qpackBlockedStreams: 16)
        h3.timeouts.idle = .seconds(60)
        h3.timeouts.drain = .seconds(5)

        let listeners: [ServerListener] = [
            .byteStream(name: "https") { bind in
                try TCPListener(configuration: .init(host: "127.0.0.1", port: 8443),
                                tls: TLSConfiguration(identity: identity, alpn: bind.alpnTokens))
            },
            .multiplexed(name: "h3", protocol: HTTP3(configuration: h3)) { bind in
                // The HTTPS port number, over UDP.
                try QUICListener(configuration: .init(host: "127.0.0.1", port: bind.boundAddresses[0].port,
                                                      quic: QUICConfiguration(alpn: bind.alpnTokens)),
                                 identity: identity)
            },
        ]
        let server = Server(listeners: listeners, protocols: [TLSNegotiated(HTTP2(), fallback: HTTP1())]) {
            altSvc
            files
        }
        try await withThrowingDiscardingTaskGroup { group in
            group.addTask { try await server.run() }
            group.addTask {
                let addresses = try await server.waitUntilRunning()   // in listener order
                altSvc.advertise(port: addresses[1].port)
                for address in addresses { print("listening \(address)") }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

This snippet type-checks against this checkout (2026-11-13). Add the SIGINT/SIGTERM
handling from `Examples/custom-server/Sources/MySite/MySite.swift` for a graceful drain.

- `bind.alpnTokens` for a multiplexed listener is the protocol's own tokens (`["h3"]`).
- `bind.boundAddresses` lets the QUIC listener take the TLS listener's port, which matters
  when that was 0.
- Put `AltSvc` first so error pages and every other response carry it.
- To reuse `http-config.json` and only add routes, see
  [Reuse http-config.json](https://photon-http.sstools.co/docs/choosing-components.md#reuse-http-configjson-and-add-your-own-routes);
  the executable's `makeListeners` shows how it adds the TLS and QUIC listeners.

## Testing it

The system curl (`/usr/bin/curl`) has no HTTP/3. Homebrew's does (ngtcp2 and nghttp3):

```bash
scripts/make-test-identity.sh             # .test-identity/server.p12, self-signed, memory-only use
swift build -j 2 --product photon
scripts/guarded.sh -t 120 -- .build/debug/photon --config Root/http-config.tls.json
```

In another terminal (`Root/http-config.tls.json` uses TCP and UDP 8443):

```bash
curl -sk -o /dev/null -D - https://127.0.0.1:8443/ | grep -i alt-svc
# alt-svc: h3=":8443"; ma=86400

/opt/homebrew/opt/curl/bin/curl --http3-only -sk -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version} %{http_code}\n' https://127.0.0.1:8443/
# 3 200
```

`--http3-only` fails rather than falling back to TCP, so a `3` proves QUIC was used; `--http3`
tries QUIC and falls back. `-k` accepts the self-signed test certificate without changing any
trust settings. Browsers need a trusted certificate before they will use the `Alt-Svc`
alternative; see the TLS guide.

These checks were run against a loopback server with the test identity on 2026-11-13: the
HTTPS response (HTTP/2) carried `alt-svc: h3=":PORT"; ma=600` as configured, `--http3-only`
got `HTTP/3 200` with no `alt-svc` header, a cleartext response had none, and SIGINT stopped
the server cleanly.

### The test suites

| Suite | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `HTTP3Tests` (in-memory) | Frame parser, control streams, connection state, request streams, limits, abuse limits, cancellation, shutdown, priorities, QPACK dynamic table, WebSockets, proxying, Alt-Svc. Driven over `InMemoryMultiplexedTransport`, so close codes are checked exactly |
